other_moves.detail: We announce that the next single-aisle will carry CFM plus at least one second source, and invite Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce and CFM to propose engines (code 7). The aim is supply certainty and customer choice; the code does not change our payoff. We revisit the code in 2035, before entry into service, against Wagner's criteria: published ready dates for GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine against the NGSA entry year; CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan; Boeing's fps code; and A320 engine delivery performance [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Secure NGSA supply first, by owning or locking it
other_moves.detail: Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: engines, then the rate-capable wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths. This follows our Spirit, titanium and rare-earth de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063], and it is for our own programme and ramp only. Announced as strengthening a more sovereign European aerospace supply chain.

other_moves.move: Ring-fence the A320 ramp from NGSA development
other_moves.detail: This is Wagner's condition for his ramp-shield pass. A320 line staffing and supplier slots are protected from NGSA development, because talent binds both [A-0366, A-0485]. Rate 75 stays the operating priority under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010, AX-0054]. The ramp is reported to the ExCo every quarter.

other_moves.move: Open recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: A public European hiring programme in engineering for NGSA, sized so as not to draw on A320 ramp staff. It is ordinary hiring and not a Delay Tactics move.

other_moves.move: Gated NGSA cash control with the Audit Committee
other_moves.detail: Headroom to the $5.2B one-year-FCF line is only $0.13B (2.5%). The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) tracks NGSA spend against the line every year. Any of the following triggers a re-phasing inside the programme, never an acceleration: a forecast overrun above $0.88B; a peak year more than 2.5% above the average; or the euro below about $1.07. Any breach comes back to the Board as an item [AX-0104, AX-0008].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation inside the policy
other_moves.detail: The dividend stays inside the 30-50% payout policy, with no equity raise. State support (refundable advances) is upside and outside the case. Toepfer's stress case leaves net cash positive to 2036 at a payout up to about 36%. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. The Audit Committee reviews this every year against actual FCF [AX-0102, AX-0001].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine kept in reserve
other_moves.detail: No launch while NGSA spends. When it returns, it comes as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column, after the A350F and Spirit absorption, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). On Toepfer's cash test the first year that passes is 2037, so the 2045 round [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

airbus.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We are launching it on its technology clock. Entry into service is planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies have matured, and not before.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it are protected.

We have invited all three engine makers to propose engines for the new aircraft. Our aim is CFM and at least one other maker on the aircraft, to give customers choice and to secure supply. We will also strengthen the European supply chain behind this programme. Securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths remains a priority.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We will fund this investment within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we will keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
**Decision.** Launch NGSA in 2030 with engine code 7. Hold the A350. No Delay Tactics.

This is plan A, the company default for the last year of the window. It is one Board item, the NGSA launch, on a Qualified Majority, with the engine code riding with it.

I applied the team rule in order, on the brief's grid, which matches both memos and the Board's figures.

**Step 1. Delete red-line breaches, whatever their PV.**
- Plan C (NGSA + A350 Re-engine) breaks rule 6. It is two launches in one round, with five overlap years and $3B of strain. The $1B exception fails at -2.15 in S5 and S6 [A-0343, A-0401]. The Board also vetoes it.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted:
  - rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so a move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine, -15.74 against A in S1 and S5;
  - bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar [AX-0073, AX-0081];
  - poaching on the NGSA-hold rows also breaks rule 5;
  - the Board vetoes all three this round.
- The rows with NGSA held and the A350 Re-engine plus Delay Tactics fall on the same grounds.

**Step 2. Survivors that pass both tests.**
- Plan A passes every test from Toepfer and Wagner.
- Plan B (hold + hold, the order default) fails Toepfer's robustness test: -4.99 in S3, negative in five of six columns.
- Plan D (NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine) fails Toepfer's robustness test (-4.80 in S6) and Wagner's A350F and Spirit absorption test.
- Neither B nor D comes within $19B of A in any column, so no override question arises. A is the only survivor.

**Step 3. Choose.** A is the highest survivor in my expected scenario, S2, at +23.37. It is also the company default, so the $1B default test is met trivially. Doctrine premium: $0.

**What the red lines cost, for the record.** These gaps are the price of the red lines, not a premium:
- S1: $1.75B below plan C.
- S2: $3.30B below C plus one Delay Tactics move.
- S3: $3.77B below the same row.
- S4: $3.30B below the same row.
- S5: none. A is the best plan.
- S6: $1.57B below A plus one Delay Tactics move.

**Step 4. Tie-breaks.** Not needed: no two survivors are within $1B. A also meets all of them: no early entry into service (2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year); zero concurrency; one Board item.

**Expected scenario: S2** (fps on a 10-year ramp, entering service 2040).
- Boeing ties a new aircraft to technology maturity "not before '35" [A-0570], to finished development programmes and to a restored balance sheet [A-0726, A-0785]. A 10-year ramp fits all three.
- The profile's prior (section 7) puts fps no earlier than 2035, which points to S1. A is the same choice there and is worth more (+45.82).
- The worst plausible column is S3, at +17.28. A stays positive in every column, and NGSA's item value against hold is +22.27 to +45.82.
- A 737 Rate Increase is not a column. It changes no programme (profile section 5, row 7).

**Own clock.** I chose 2030 because it is the last year of the 2028-2030 window, with entry into service in 2037, "around 2037" and "the second half of the next decade" [AX-0020, A-0409, AX-0006]. Boeing's possible moves did not set the year. Whatever Boeing does in 2030, NGSA moves neither earlier nor later and is never cancelled in reaction (rules 2 and 7).

**The NGSA bill.** $35.52B (dashboard_game section 2) governs. The $30.07B on the earlier cards, my own included, cannot be traced in the current mapping. At $30.07B, headroom would rise to $0.90B and no result would change.

**Peak cash is thin.** Spend is $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against about $5.2B, headroom $0.13B (2.5%). Any one of these breaks the line:
- a total overrun above $0.88B;
- uneven phasing, with any year more than 2.5% above the average;
- a euro below about $1.07.

So I attach Audit Committee monitoring, with re-phasing, never acceleration, as the remedy (my supply-binds reflex [AX-0054]).

**Returns.** The payout stays inside the 30-50% policy with no equity raise. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. I am bringing that to the Board openly as a flag, not hiding it.

**A350 Re-engine.** Kept in reserve. Wagner's capacity test would pass a 2035 launch (two years of overlap, $1.2B of strain). Toepfer's peak-cash test fails any launch before 2037 ($6.67B a year). Peak cash is the Board's line, so the CFO's test governs. On present numbers the earliest launch is the 2045 round, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).

**Delay Tactics.** Off. I do not set aside the team's stricter condition that the move must change who enters service first. On this board a move shifts share, not entry into service, so the condition keeps it off. Toepfer's preview also shows a 2035 move breaking the cash line while NGSA spends.

**Engine code: 7.** Both colleagues and the Board recommend CFM plus a second maker. Only a P&W or RR engine launched this round can be ready by 2037. Code 7 selects both, CFM backstops, and code 7 is in no barred pair [A-0243, A-0360].

**Overrides.** None.

**Board-gate line: `ngsa: launch` (2030, entry into service 2037), Qualified Majority [AG-0049, AX-0026], engine code 7 riding with it.**
- Five pillars: pass. Wagner confirms safety and quality; the public line gives windows, not dates, and no covert move.
- Toepfer's tests: pass. Peak $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B (headroom $0.13B). Robustness worst case S3 at +17.28. Payout inside policy, no equity raise, state support outside the case.
- Wagner's tests: pass on safety, quality, A320 ramp shield (with the ring-fence), production readiness and engineering capacity (zero overlap). Supply crunch: not applicable.
- Grid ΔPV, S1 to S6: +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51.
- Item value against hold + hold: +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67. It never loses $2B in any column.

airbus.objective_note:
The briefing goal is "Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family". The GM scores it; it does not change the payoff, and I trade no PV for it.

On plan A, by column:
- S1 and S5: NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year from 2037 (cap 80%). The edge is met in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- S2, S4 and S6: a three-year lead (2037 against 2040), about 63% Airbus by 2040, then convergence toward a 47/53 long-run split. The edge is met in 2040 and missed in 2045 and 2050.
- S3: the same entry year, with Boeing climbing toward 50/50. Missed from about 2040.

Protect the A320 family is met in every column, unless Boeing orders a 737 Rate Increase. That moves Airbus to about 55% in 2032-36, a miss no Airbus order on this board can prevent. Our answer is our own disciplined ramp, not a programme move.

The only order that would lift the objective (Delay Tactics, 5 pp for 5 years from fps entry into service) is struck on red lines. So no premium is sized for the objective.

frame.situation:
Round 1, decision year 2030.

Public record:

- Observed shares for 2026-2029 are the status quo: Airbus 60% of narrowbody, 41.2% of widebody.

Our objective ("Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family") is met on the hold path, with a worst year of 60.0%. The hold path is not safe, though. Do Nothing scores 0.00 only if Boeing also holds. If Boeing moves (S2-S6) it scores -0.86 to -4.99.

2030 is the last year of the NGSA window. Launched now, NGSA enters service in 2037, consistent with "around 2037" and "the second half of the next decade" [A-0409, AX-0020, dashboard_game section 5].

We do not know Boeing's intentions. The grid's S1-S6 are its plausible orders, and the bulletin rules none out.
- My provisional expectation is S2: an fps launched on a 10-year ramp, entering service in 2040. Boeing ties a new aircraft to repairing its balance sheet and to "not before 2035" (profile section 7, a prior and not a script). I will confirm the scenario at decide.
- The worst plausible column for an NGSA plan is S3: fps on a 7-year ramp, entering service in 2037, the same year as NGSA.
- A 737 Rate Increase (2030-only order) is not one of the six columns. Our reaction to it is no programme change (profile section 5, row 7).

No Boeing fps is on the public record, so any Delay Tactics would be naked and would draw the $48.32B fine.

The Board's guidance (risk aversion 4 of 5, horizon 4 of 5) asks for:

ops.would_change_mind_if: (1) A brief reporting a supply crunch, an A320 quality escape or a ramp problem: I would re-test NGSA against the ramp shield and the supply test and block any concurrency. NGSA would still not be cancelled. (2) An engine maturity slip: re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year, and never cancel it. It also needs an overlap with NGSA of 2 years or less (a 2035 launch, $1.2B strain) or a grid gain of at least $1B in every plausible column, one launch per round, and no 787 Re-engine on the record (rule 3). ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived; confidence Very low. Nothing of mine is on record.

Plan A passes every operating test. Safety and quality: NGSA launched in 2030, EIS 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year, stands on the five pillars; the brief reports no quality, ramp or supply problem. Ramp shield: rate 75 was due stable from end-2027; NGSA spend from 2030 does not compete with it, provided A320 staff and supplier slots stay ring-fenced. Readiness: 2030 is the last window year.

Capacity: NGSA holds the shared engineering teams 2030-2037. Plan C is two launches in one round, five overlap years, $3B strain, and its gain turns to -2.15 in S5 and S6: rule 6, deleted. Any A350 Re-engine in round 1 also fails A350F and Spirit absorption (C and D, binding soft veto; D trails A by $19.0-46.5B). Earliest pass on my side: 2035, two years' overlap, $1.2B strain, at the limit. Peak cash is Thomas's call.

Engines: code 7. Only a P&W or RR engine launched this round can be ready by 2037 (GTF2 or Joint Venture 2036, UltraFan 2037). Code 7 selects both; CFM backstops. Before 2035 I want the published ready dates, CFM's engine choice and A320 engine deliveries.

Supply first: engines, then the rate-capable wing packages, titanium forgings, rare earths.

Delay Tactics: off. No fps on the record, so rule 4 bars every move; bottleneck and both breach integrity.

Boeing's Rate Increase changes nothing: our ramp stays disciplined and controlled.

other_moves.move: NGSA engine competition open to all three makers
other_moves.detail: We announce that the next single-aisle will carry CFM plus at least one second source, and invite Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce and CFM to propose engines (code 7). The aim is supply certainty and customer choice; the code does not change our payoff. We revisit the code in 2035, before entry into service, against Wagner's criteria: published ready dates for GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine against the NGSA entry year; CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan; Boeing's fps code; and A320 engine delivery performance [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Secure NGSA supply first, by owning or locking it
other_moves.detail: Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: engines, then the rate-capable wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths. This follows our Spirit, titanium and rare-earth de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063], and it is for our own programme and ramp only. Announced as strengthening a more sovereign European aerospace supply chain.

other_moves.move: Ring-fence the A320 ramp from NGSA development
other_moves.detail: This is Wagner's condition for his ramp-shield pass. A320 line staffing and supplier slots are protected from NGSA development, because talent binds both [A-0366, A-0485]. Rate 75 stays the operating priority under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010, AX-0054]. The ramp is reported to the ExCo every quarter.

other_moves.move: Open recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: A public European hiring programme in engineering for NGSA, sized so as not to draw on A320 ramp staff. It is ordinary hiring and not a Delay Tactics move.

other_moves.move: Gated NGSA cash control with the Audit Committee
other_moves.detail: Headroom to the $5.2B one-year-FCF line is only $0.13B (2.5%). The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) tracks NGSA spend against the line every year. Any of the following triggers a re-phasing inside the programme, never an acceleration: a forecast overrun above $0.88B; a peak year more than 2.5% above the average; or the euro below about $1.07. Any breach comes back to the Board as an item [AX-0104, AX-0008].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation inside the policy
other_moves.detail: The dividend stays inside the 30-50% payout policy, with no equity raise. State support (refundable advances) is upside and outside the case. Toepfer's stress case leaves net cash positive to 2036 at a payout up to about 36%. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. The Audit Committee reviews this every year against actual FCF [AX-0102, AX-0001].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine kept in reserve
other_moves.detail: No launch while NGSA spends. When it returns, it comes as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column, after the A350F and Spirit absorption, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). On Toepfer's cash test the first year that passes is 2037, so the 2045 round [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We are launching it on its technology clock. Entry into service is planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies have matured, and not before.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it are protected.

We have invited all three engine makers to propose engines for the new aircraft. Our aim is CFM and at least one other maker on the aircraft, to give customers choice and to secure supply. We will also strengthen the European supply chain behind this programme. Securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths remains a priority.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We will fund this investment within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we will keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
**Decision.** Launch NGSA in 2030 with engine code 7. Hold the A350. No Delay Tactics.

This is plan A, the company default for the last year of the window. It is one Board item, the NGSA launch, on a Qualified Majority, with the engine code riding with it.

I applied the team rule in order, on the brief's grid, which matches both memos and the Board's figures.

**Step 1. Delete red-line breaches, whatever their PV.**
- Plan C (NGSA + A350 Re-engine) breaks rule 6. It is two launches in one round, with five overlap years and $3B of strain. The $1B exception fails at -2.15 in S5 and S6 [A-0343, A-0401]. The Board also vetoes it.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted:
  - rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so a move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine, -15.74 against A in S1 and S5;
  - bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar [AX-0073, AX-0081];
  - poaching on the NGSA-hold rows also breaks rule 5;
  - the Board vetoes all three this round.
- The rows with NGSA held and the A350 Re-engine plus Delay Tactics fall on the same grounds.

**Step 2. Survivors that pass both tests.**
- Plan A passes every test from Toepfer and Wagner.
- Plan B (hold + hold, the order default) fails Toepfer's robustness test: -4.99 in S3, negative in five of six columns.
- Plan D (NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine) fails Toepfer's robustness test (-4.80 in S6) and Wagner's A350F and Spirit absorption test.
- Neither B nor D comes within $19B of A in any column, so no override question arises. A is the only survivor.

**Step 3. Choose.** A is the highest survivor in my expected scenario, S2, at +23.37. It is also the company default, so the $1B default test is met trivially. Doctrine premium: $0.

**What the red lines cost, for the record.** These gaps are the price of the red lines, not a premium:
- S1: $1.75B below plan C.
- S2: $3.30B below C plus one Delay Tactics move.
- S3: $3.77B below the same row.
- S4: $3.30B below the same row.
- S5: none. A is the best plan.
- S6: $1.57B below A plus one Delay Tactics move.

**Step 4. Tie-breaks.** Not needed: no two survivors are within $1B. A also meets all of them: no early entry into service (2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year); zero concurrency; one Board item.

**Expected scenario: S2** (fps on a 10-year ramp, entering service 2040).
- Boeing ties a new aircraft to technology maturity "not before '35" [A-0570], to finished development programmes and to a restored balance sheet [A-0726, A-0785]. A 10-year ramp fits all three.
- The profile's prior (section 7) puts fps no earlier than 2035, which points to S1. A is the same choice there and is worth more (+45.82).
- The worst plausible column is S3, at +17.28. A stays positive in every column, and NGSA's item value against hold is +22.27 to +45.82.
- A 737 Rate Increase is not a column. It changes no programme (profile section 5, row 7).

**Own clock.** I chose 2030 because it is the last year of the 2028-2030 window, with entry into service in 2037, "around 2037" and "the second half of the next decade" [AX-0020, A-0409, AX-0006]. Boeing's possible moves did not set the year. Whatever Boeing does in 2030, NGSA moves neither earlier nor later and is never cancelled in reaction (rules 2 and 7).

**The NGSA bill.** $35.52B (dashboard_game section 2) governs. The $30.07B on the earlier cards, my own included, cannot be traced in the current mapping. At $30.07B, headroom would rise to $0.90B and no result would change.

**Peak cash is thin.** Spend is $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against about $5.2B, headroom $0.13B (2.5%). Any one of these breaks the line:
- a total overrun above $0.88B;
- uneven phasing, with any year more than 2.5% above the average;
- a euro below about $1.07.

So I attach Audit Committee monitoring, with re-phasing, never acceleration, as the remedy (my supply-binds reflex [AX-0054]).

**Returns.** The payout stays inside the 30-50% policy with no equity raise. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. I am bringing that to the Board openly as a flag, not hiding it.

**A350 Re-engine.** Kept in reserve. Wagner's capacity test would pass a 2035 launch (two years of overlap, $1.2B of strain). Toepfer's peak-cash test fails any launch before 2037 ($6.67B a year). Peak cash is the Board's line, so the CFO's test governs. On present numbers the earliest launch is the 2045 round, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).

**Delay Tactics.** Off. I do not set aside the team's stricter condition that the move must change who enters service first. On this board a move shifts share, not entry into service, so the condition keeps it off. Toepfer's preview also shows a 2035 move breaking the cash line while NGSA spends.

**Engine code: 7.** Both colleagues and the Board recommend CFM plus a second maker. Only a P&W or RR engine launched this round can be ready by 2037. Code 7 selects both, CFM backstops, and code 7 is in no barred pair [A-0243, A-0360].

**Overrides.** None.

**Board-gate line: `ngsa: launch` (2030, entry into service 2037), Qualified Majority [AG-0049, AX-0026], engine code 7 riding with it.**
- Five pillars: pass. Wagner confirms safety and quality; the public line gives windows, not dates, and no covert move.
- Toepfer's tests: pass. Peak $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B (headroom $0.13B). Robustness worst case S3 at +17.28. Payout inside policy, no equity raise, state support outside the case.
- Wagner's tests: pass on safety, quality, A320 ramp shield (with the ring-fence), production readiness and engineering capacity (zero overlap). Supply crunch: not applicable.
- Grid ΔPV, S1 to S6: +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51.
- Item value against hold + hold: +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67. It never loses $2B in any column.
decision.expected_scenario:
S2: Boeing launches fps on a 10-year ramp (entry into service 2040), with no 787 Re-engine this round. This keeps the provisional reading from my framing. It fits Boeing's "not before '35" technology clock and balance-sheet preconditions [A-0570, A-0726, A-0785].

S1 (rivals hold, per the profile's prior that fps comes no earlier than 2035) is the close alternative. Plan A is the same choice there and is worth +45.82.

The worst plausible column is S3 (fps on a 7-year ramp, entering service 2037), at +17.28.

A 737 Rate Increase is likely [A-0820] but is not a column.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:
In S2 the best grid row is NGSA + A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics (one move), at +26.67. It is deleted on company red lines (rule 6: two launches; rule 4: a naked move with no fps on the record) and on the Board's veto.

The best surviving plan is NGSA + A350: hold, at +23.37. That is $3.30B below the deleted row, a red-line cost and not a doctrine premium. It is also the company default and the order submitted.
decision.premium_reason:
No doctrine premium is paid. The submitted plan is the company default and the best plan that survives the red lines and both colleagues' tests in the expected scenario.

The $3.30B gap in S2 to the unconstrained best row is the cost of red lines (rules 4 and 6, integrity), which are never traded for PV. It is not a premium inside the $1B or $3B allowances.

No PV is traded for the briefing objective.
decision.objective_note:
The briefing goal is "Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family". The GM scores it; it does not change the payoff, and I trade no PV for it.

On plan A, by column:
- S1 and S5: NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year from 2037 (cap 80%). The edge is met in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- S2, S4 and S6: a three-year lead (2037 against 2040), about 63% Airbus by 2040, then convergence toward a 47/53 long-run split. The edge is met in 2040 and missed in 2045 and 2050.
- S3: the same entry year, with Boeing climbing toward 50/50. Missed from about 2040.

Protect the A320 family is met in every column, unless Boeing orders a 737 Rate Increase. That moves Airbus to about 55% in 2032-36, a miss no Airbus order on this board can prevent. Our answer is our own disciplined ramp, not a programme move.

The only order that would lift the objective (Delay Tactics, 5 pp for 5 years from fps entry into service) is struck on red lines. So no premium is sized for the objective.
decision.predictions:
Boeing, 2030:
- A 737 Rate Increase is likely (sold out, raising rates [A-0820]).
- On fps, S2 (10-year ramp) is my modal case, with a hold (S1) a close second. A 7-year launch (S3) is possible if Boeing reacts to our window [A-0035].
- No 787 Re-engine this round: its widebody focus is the 777X and 787 rate.

Engine makers:
- Our code 7 lets P&W's and RR's launch_if_selected orders trigger: GTF2 ready 2036 and UltraFan NB ready 2037, so either could be fitted at NGSA entry into service.
- A P&W-RR Joint Venture is possible.
- CFM is likely to pursue a ducted engine, with Open Fan not before 2045.

Market: no narrowbody share change before 2037 unless Boeing raises its rate, in which case Boeing gains +5 pp in 2032-36.

2035 bulletin: NGSA on the record (entry into service 2037), with Boeing's fps status known. In round 2:
- any Delay Tactics question would be reassessed under the Board's conditions, with Toepfer's preview already showing a 2035 move breaking the cash line;
- the engine code is revisited on published ready dates;
- the A350 Re-engine stays in reserve on cash.

Expected ΔPV (S2, nobody moves after this round): +23.37. Range +17.28 (S3) to +45.82 (S1).

2. Robustness: pass.

items.ground:
The Board approves this item. It is above EUR 800m, so the Board read it as a Qualified Majority item [AG-0049, AG-0011], and the papers set out both the finance case and the industrial case. Every test that touches the item passes on the round1.md grid.

(2) Technology clock. The launch is in 2030, the last year of the 2028-2030 window. Entry into service is 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year [A-0225, A-0409, AG-0063].

(3) Downside. The item value against hold + hold is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67 across S1 to S6. That is +26.67 in the CEO's expected scenario, S2, and a gain in every plausible column. The submitted row stays positive even in its worst column, S3 at +17.28 [AX-0007, AG-0029, A-0364].

(4) Liquidity and rating. At $35.52B / 7, spend is $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against the $5.2B line, a pass with $0.13B (2.5%) of headroom. The Board uses the dashboard bill in place of the $30.07B on its own card, as its card instructs [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, AX-0104].

(5) One clean sheet. There is one launch, with 0 years of overlap and $0 of strain [A-0343].

(6) Safety and ramp. Wagner passes the plan on safety, quality and the A320 ramp shield, with the ring-fence adopted. The supply-crunch test does not apply [AX-0015, AG-0038, A-0331, A-0303].

(7) Returns kept fundable. The plan passes the liquidity test. The buyback ends in 2029, before NGSA cash starts. No equity raise is needed and state money is outside the case [AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0034].

(8) Engine code. Code 7 keeps CFM plus a second maker. This is not a veto matter [A-0243, A-0360].

recommendations.text: Cash gate. The Board endorses the gate. Each year the Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) should review NGSA spend against the $5.2B line, which is one year's FCF. The Board's papers now carry the $35.52B bill in place of the card's $30.07B. Any one of these break points comes back to the Board as an item: a total overrun above $0.88B; a peak year more than 2.5% above the average; the euro below about $1.07; or any Delay Tactics spend. Re-phasing inside the programme is the remedy. It must not accelerate the programme or move entry into service from 2037.

Dividend and rating. The Board proposes the dividend each year. The CFO's stress case (flat FCF, the full bill treated as incremental, no customer advances) keeps net cash positive to 2036 only at a payout of up to about 36%. Holding EUR 3.20 a share needs FCF of about $5.9B; without it, net debt reaches about $5B by 2036. For the 2035 round the Board asks the CFO for a base case beside the stress case, and for the A+/A1 headroom metrics his memo does not contain. He should also confirm that no equity raise, and no dividend cut outside a crisis, is required. State support, refundable advances included, stays upside only.

A350 Re-engine in reserve. On the Board's liquidity line, any launch before NGSA cash rolls off peaks at about $6.67B a year. The first launch year that passes is therefore 2037, which is the 2045 round. Wagner's 2035 capacity pass (2 years of overlap, $1.2B of strain) is noted, but liquidity governs. If the 2035 bulletin shows a 787 Re-engine (S5 or S6), rule 3 bars the A350 Re-engine. Any return should come as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column.

Delay Tactics stay none. Bottleneck and both remain integrity vetoes in any round. Poaching becomes reviewable only if all of these hold: Boeing's fps is public and not in service; NGSA is in development; it is the only move of the game; it is at least $1B ahead in the expected column; and the CEO has recorded setting aside the team's stricter condition. The Board also notes the CFO's preview. A 2035 move against an fps entering service in 2040 adds about $0.20B a year and lifts peak spend to about $5.27B. That is over the $5.2B line, so while NGSA spends at $5.07B a year the move would also fail the Board's liquidity test.

Other moves, within integrity limits. The supply agreements (engines, wing packages, titanium, rare earths) must be sized to Airbus's own NGSA and A320 needs. They must never be over-contracted to deny capacity to a rival, because that would be a bottleneck, which the Board vetoes on integrity. Public engineering hiring must not draw on A320 ramp staff and must never target Boeing's fps teams, because that would be poaching, a Board item. The Board asks the ECSC to review both once a year.

Safety and ramp. The A320 ring-fence and the quarterly ramp report to the ExCo are noted. The Board's twice-yearly safety review should take the A320 ramp report and NGSA development readiness together. That way a quality escape or a supply crunch reaches the Board before it reaches the cash line.

Reaction discipline for 2035. Whatever Boeing ordered in 2030 (an fps on any ramp, a 787 Re-engine or a 737 Rate Increase), NGSA stays on its 2037 clock. The Board would consider cancelling NGSA only if continuing lost at least $1B in every plausible column. On this grid NGSA gains in every column.

Engine supply. Code 7 is noted: CFM plus a second maker, and never in a barred pair. Revisit the code before 2035 against published engine-ready dates (GTF2 or a Joint Venture engine ready 2036, UltraFan NB ready 2037), CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan, and A320 engine deliveries. The code is not a veto ground.

Public statement. The draft follows the Board's guidance: the five pillars come first, entry into service is given as 'the second half of the 2030s', there are no long-term-plan targets, and Delay Tactics are not mentioned. The Board vets the final text before release.

board_review.note: The Board approves its only item, ngsa: launch in 2030 with engine code 7, read as a Qualified Majority item. Every test that touches it passes on the round1.md grid. Its item value against hold is +22.27 to +45.82 in all six columns, and the plan's worst column is S3 at +17.28. Peak spend is $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line. It is one programme with no overlap. Entry into service is 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. Wagner passes it on safety, quality and the ramp. Both colleagues concur, and no override was made. The A350 hold and Delay Tactics none are defaults, not Board items. The Board names two risks: cash headroom is only $0.13B (2.5%), and in the CFO's stress case the EUR 3.20 dividend needs FCF near $5.9B. Both go to the Audit Committee as recommendations; neither is a veto ground. Supply agreements and hiring stand only within the integrity limits set out.

other_moves.detail: Publish entry into service in 2040, no earlier, as a planning baseline with buffer in it. State the risk case as a condition: a supply-chain or engineering-talent disruption around EIS. On the board that is S5: 5 pp of share lost for 5 years from EIS, -0.78 against Do Nothing's -3.64. Keep any earlier internal date as upside and never publish it. If the date moves, reset once and say so early [BX-0553, BX-1318, BX-1306].

other_moves.detail: Contract fps development on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]. This is not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Certify before building at rate
other_moves.detail: The fps program plan carries no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]. The 10-year ramp leaves room to certify before the line goes to rate.

other_moves.move: Fund from operations and debt capacity; keep deleveraging
other_moves.detail: No new equity. Stay solidly investment grade on the 10-year phasing, about $6.0B a year over 2030-39 against $6.7B a year of airplane operating profit (Malave's arithmetic). Debt stays the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327].

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: Fund fragile suppliers so they stay above our rate as the fps ramp loads the same base as the 737 at 47 a month. Embed staff, buffer, requalify; acquire if needed [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2264]. Attribute no bottleneck to anyone before exposure.

other_moves.move: Engine request: code 3 (CFM), durability first
other_moves.detail: Request CFM. It is always available by 2040, as a LEAP derivative at worst. Require a matured engine before EIS, with durability proven on the ground [BX-1298, BX-1325], and watch CFM's load across both airframers' rates [BX-1264]. If NGSA also takes code 3, the board moves the later airframe to code 7 at no change in payoff.

other_moves.move: Independent estimate check and early-warning rule
other_moves.detail: Malave reviews the fps estimate and schedule independently every quarter [BX-1316]. Any slip is reported early with the mitigation attached, and costed once in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost [B-2349, BX-1299].

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine parked to 2035 on conditions; widebody growth from Charleston
other_moves.detail: Bring the Re-engine back in Round 2 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half) and its overlap with the fps is no more than 2 years (H4). Until then, widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336].

boeing.public_statement:
When I started, I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We've spent these years earning that. The 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are delivering. Our production lines are stable on the KPIs. Our balance sheet is healthier. I think we've turned this ship. I don't think the work is done.

Today we are launching a new single-aisle airplane. It is a Boeing airplane, and we will own the design. We are taking the ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. That is a planning date with headroom built in, not a stretch target. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We have tested the plan against a harder case, including disruption in the supply chain or our engineering workforce around entry into service, and it still stands. If the schedule moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

A few things will not change. We will certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll share risk with our suppliers on terms that work for both of us, and we'll keep the supply chain funded and healthy. We'll fund this from our operations and our debt capacity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

We are not changing production rates today. The 737 stays where its KPIs have it, and we are not starting a second development alongside this one. Doing less, and doing it better, is what got us here.

This decision rests on our own readiness, not on anyone else's timeline. The financials will follow our production performance. We have a lot of work in front of us, and we're going to do it one step at a time.
boeing.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 1 (2030), team rule of teams.md §9: I propose and decide; Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can block.

1. Vetoes in force. Malave holds one binding veto: every fps launch_via_embraer row fails his slip leg. In S5 they score -18.83, -17.47, -19.58 and -18.21, against a floor of -5.64 (Do Nothing -3.64). Embraer is out and I do not contest it. Pope ran the KPI check on a Rate Increase and did not invoke her veto: the brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's H4 flag on fps 7-yr + Re-engine (5 years of overlap) is correct; that row is struck. Neither colleague vetoes the 10-year Solo, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live problem, with 800 narrowbody and 100 widebody deliveries a year, flat over 2026-29. 47 a month cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069] is company record, not in the brief.
- Market, technology and Boeing ready?
  - Market: waiting is not free. Do Nothing scores -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 if Airbus moves.
  - Technology: H2 cannot bind; EIS 2040 is well after 2035.
  - Boeing: see the H1 ruling below.
- If certification takes longer? Read S5 first. The 10-year scores -0.78 there, +2.86 against Do Nothing and 4.86 above the floor.
- Doing less, better? The 10-year Solo beats Do Nothing by +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86 in S1-S5, so it is above ε in every column. It carries the smallest bill of the launches.

3. H1 ruling (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were unfinished developments and unrepaired debt [B-2326, BX-1305], and they no longer hold:
- the 777X is delivering from 2027 [BX-0550];
- the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299];
- 777X cash was near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes for a 2030 launch;
- debt repair ran on the path I set at Farnborough, about two more years with a launch around 2029-30 [BG-0068, B-2327];
- Spirit is inside [BG-0064].
The post-2025 outcomes rest on the teams.md §9 script and Board-file record, not on my own words, and the brief reports no certification trouble. My FAA-process gate [BX-1309] therefore passes.

4. H3 ruling, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): held on a re-founded ground. The literal 2026 ground (the 777X first) has lapsed. The principle has not: one major development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], finish what is in hand first [B-2326], do less and do it better [BX-1239]. From 2030 the program in hand is the fps. The Board's Downside test also bars the Re-engine: -3.58 in S3 and S4 beside the 10-year. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written.

5. The ramp, my main call. In my expected column S4 (doctrine's reading of Airbus, profile §7; my own confidence on Airbus is Low), C (7-year) scores -1.50 and B (10-year) -1.96. That is 0.46 apart, inside ε, so doctrine breaks the tie. I take the 10-year:
- Doing less [BX-1239]: the bill is $4.68B smaller ($60.32B against $65.00B). The undiscounted debt penalty is $2.9B lower ($19.1B against $22.0B; Malave confirms the 16.3/21.7 set on my card is stale), about $2.6B lower discounted.
- Headroom [BX-1275, B-2295, BX-1241]: about $6.0B a year of spend against about $9.3B. The 7-year would need about $2.6B a year borrowed above airplane operating profit. Malave supports the rating only on the 10-year phasing.
- Honest date: Pope's clean-sheet slip prior (central +3 years, doctrine) puts a 7-year launch at 2040 anyway. So 2040 is a date we can meet and maybe beat [BX-0553].
- Robustness: B leads C by 1.30 in S1 and S3 and by 0.05 in S5, and trails by only 0.46 in S2 and S4. Its five-column mean is +0.46 against +0.11.
- Airbus does not set the date [B-2313]. The 7-year's one structural edge is entering service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched in 2030. Choosing it for that edge would time our airplane to theirs, which I will not do.
I log 0.46 as a doctrine premium, within the $2B cap. The Board recommended the 7-year for its higher worst column. I take that seriously, but the 10-year's worst column (-1.96) is still $4.30B above Do Nothing's in the same column. Doctrine (profile §11.4) tilts the same way as my record here.

6. Rate Increase: hold. Beside any fps launch its item value is -0.74 in every column (B 3.50 / 0.66 / 0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78 becomes 2.76 / -0.08 / 0.14 / -2.70 / -1.52). It fails the value condition and the Board's business case. Declining in 2030 is final, but it costs nothing in any column beside the fps. Airbus played no part in this reasoning (H6).

7. Embraer: out on Malave's binding veto and Pope's IP test. It costs $39.68B more bill for the same 2040 EIS.

8. Board items and rows.
- fps launch_10yr (with code 3 riding with it). Submitted row: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. With the item at its default (Do Nothing): 0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. Item value: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. It is above $1B in the expected column, never below -$1B, and S5 clears the floor by 4.86.
- No other Board item: the rate and the Re-engine are held.
- Premium 0.46 (S4, doctrine). Hard-rule cost from H3: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, nil in S3 and S4.

Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice: the expected column (profile §7); the re-founded H3 ground (company record on one development at a time); engine code 3 (Low on my record; doctrine and inference); the supplier-readiness and strain tests (Pope's seat is doctrine-played).

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave is my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. His seat is thin (one call, Low), so beyond the buffer test I weighed his views as advice.

- Buffer test: binding, and applied. The Embraer rows (-17.47 to -19.58 in S5) are out. B passes with -0.78, C with -0.83.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. 777X cash is positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and the launch year is 2030.
- Taken on his word:
  - the corrected debt-penalty set (19.1 / 22.0 / 52.5 undiscounted, already netted, never subtracted again; 16.3 / 21.7 is stale);
  - the funding arithmetic: about $6.0B a year on the 10-year against $6.7B of operating profit, with no new equity, and the rating supportable on the 10-year phasing standing alone;
  - the disclosure: 2040, risk case stated as a condition, earlier date held as upside.
- His 'higher worst column' rule pointed to the 7-year by 0.46. He set it aside himself on balance sheet first and logged the premium. I agree.
- His advice on the Re-engine (-3.58 in S3 and S4, side-by-side spend in 2030-34) and the Rate Increase (-0.74) matched my own holds.

I note one limit: his per-year spend is an even spread, which is inference; real programs peak mid-development.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat is played by the [NOW] operations doctrine with Very low airplane evidence. Her delivery, IP and cash tests are her record applied by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine. I weighed her memo as readiness results, which the Board requires, not as independent airplane judgment.

- KPI veto: checked and not invoked. The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. She was right to flag that the 2-3 stable months [BX-1271] and 47 a month [BG-0069] are company record I passed in, not brief data.
- Strain: the fps alone has 0 years of overlap and $0 of strain. The 10-year + Re-engine counts 2 years ($1.2B) on the board but runs side by side in 2030-35. Her H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine (5 years) is correct, and I struck that row.
- Ramp: the 10-year holds its date under doctrine's +3-year slip prior. It has less value riding on the nominal date ($1.44B lost from S2 to S5, against $1.95B), and the 7-year carries a 54% heavier annual load. That headroom finding is what kept me on the 10-year after I had said in the frame I would weigh the 7-year.
- IP: Solo; Embraer adds neither capital nor capacity.
- Engines: CFM is always available by EIS. Other makers count only with a ready date on or before EIS.
- Supplier caveat taken into other_moves: beyond 47 the supply base binds [B-2340], and the fps ramp loads the same base.

boeing.expected_scenario: S4 (Airbus launches NGSA and an A350 Re-engine), with S2 a close second. This is doctrine's reading of Airbus (profile §7); my own record on Airbus is Low. The decision does not hang on it: the 10-year Solo beats Do Nothing by more than ε in all five columns, and B and C are within ε in both S2 and S4.
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S4, the best grid row is fps 7-yr + 787: hold at -1.50. It is also the best plan that respects the hard rules and the Board's tests. My plan, fps 10-yr + 787: hold (rate hold), scores -1.96 there: 0.46 behind, inside ε, and logged as a doctrine premium. In S2 the best grid row is fps 10-yr + 787 Re-engine at +2.86, which H3 (my Round-1 ruling) and the Board's Downside test exclude; among H3-legal rows the 7-year leads at +1.12, against +0.66 for the 10-year.
boeing.objective_note:
The company's mission (objectives.md §1) is not on my ranked list and does not change the payoff.

- Hold 50/50 (Boeing NB share of 50% or more in 2040, 2045 and 2050): not met under any plan. The earliest fps EIS is 2037, and the board moves share 1 pp a year, so 2040 tops out near 43%.
- Defend incumbency (40% or more in 2030-50):
  - With the 10-year ramp it is met in S1 and S3, where Boeing climbs from 2040.
  - In S2 and S4 an NGSA entering service in 2037 would be alone for three years. On my reading of the public share rules, Boeing then falls to about 37% by 2040, before climbing toward a 47/53 long-run split, so incumbency is missed for roughly 2038-43 (inference from rules.md).
  - In S5 both ramps miss it (Delay Tactics take 5 pp from EIS).
- The 7-year would hold incumbency in S2 and S4 by entering service with NGSA. I did not take it for that, because it would time our airplane to Airbus [B-2313] and give up the headroom above.
- The objective is logged as not fully met. No PV was given up for the objective, so the objective premium is 0.
boeing.predictions:
My record gives me little on Airbus (Low), so these lean on doctrine.

Airbus:
- Most likely in 2030: an NGSA launch (S2 or S4), with roughly even odds of an A350 Re-engine alongside it.
- Any covert Delay Tactics would only show around our 2040 EIS. I attribute nothing before exposure.

Engines:
- CFM stays our available engine by 2040 under code 3. Any rival maker's new narrowbody engine counts only with a public ready date on or before 2040.

Boeing on the board, under my orders:
- Narrowbody share holds at 40% through the 2030s unless NGSA enters service in 2037. In that case it dips to about 37% by 2040, then recovers toward 47% over the 2040s once the fps is in service.

recommendations.text: Rule explicitly on H1 and H3 in the decision, citing evidence. The H1 conditions were written for 2026. By 2030 our record has the 777X reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550], the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix expected to certify in 2026 [BX-1873], 777X cash near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and debt first [B-2327]. Ortberg's own test is that market, technology and finances must all be ready [BG-0068, B-2303]. If you lift H1, say so and say why. A launch without that ruling fails our Boeing-ready test.

Show the risk-case column against Do Nothing. Do Nothing scores -3.64 in S5, so no plan may fall below -5.64. Both Solo ramps clear it (-0.83 and -0.78). Fund any launch within the investment-grade rating and from operations and debt capacity. A plan that needs new equity or puts the rating at risk will not pass this board.

On the ramp, as a risk-averse board: the two ramps are not within $1B of each other in every column. The 10-year is better by 1.30 in S1 and S3; the 7-year is better by 0.46 in S2 and S4 and by 0.05 in S5. We therefore recommend the ramp with the higher worst column: launch_7yr (worst -1.50 in S4, against -1.96 for the 10-year). Either ramp passes our tests. If you choose the 10-year, state why in the rationale. Do not choose either ramp because of Airbus's timing.

One development at a time: no 787 Re-engine this round. Its item value is -2.48 to -4.51 in the A350 Re-engine columns (S3 and S4), which this board cannot rule out, and with a 7-year fps the overlap is 5 years. Bring it back in 2035 only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3) and the overlap with fps is no more than 2 years.

Keep the Rate Increase apart from any fps launch. With fps launched, the Rate Increase is worth -0.74 in every column, and it pulls the fps item value below $1B in S1 and S3, which puts the launch itself at risk at review. If fps holds, bring the Rate Increase only on stable KPIs agreed with the FAA, with Pope's results, and with a rationale that does not cite Airbus (H6).

Log premium_b with its reason, within the $2B cap (H8). Measure it against the best plan that respects the hard rules and passes this board's tests, which this round means the Solo fps rows without a Re-engine or Rate Increase. Record any value forgone to H3 or to our Downside test separately, as a hard-rule cost, not a soft premium. Under the public share rules no plan reaches 50% of the narrowbody market by 2040, so no objective premium buys the 2040 test (inference).

Engine code: request a maker whose engine will be ready by fps EIS (2037 on the 7-year ramp, 2040 on the 10-year). CFM is always available as the fallback. A request for RR, P&W or the Joint Venture is acceptable, but say how you will judge that maker's readiness. This is not a veto ground.

Disclosure: no fps date unless fps is launched. At launch, a conservative EIS with headroom, and publish the nominal and risk-case range. Never blame the FAA or suppliers. We will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions, and we judge this choice on the long cycle.

frame.question: Is 2030 the year the three work streams finally converge? Are the market, the technology and Boeing (finances and capacity) all ready, with the 777X and MAX 7/10 behind us? If so, we lift H1 and launch one Solo fps, and I need to know on which ramp. Then: does anything else earn a place beside it (737 Rate Increase, 787 Re-engine, the Embraer route), or is this a round for doing less and doing it better? I am putting my four questions to this ExCo. (1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and I want Pope's seat to confirm it [BX-1271, BX-1259]. (2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]? (3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave's risk-case column, S5, read before we decide [BX-1319]. (4) Is each plan doing less, better when set against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239]?

I am testing it to price the H3 ruling.
