red_lines: H1 (no fps in Round 1). My provisional ruling: lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds no longer hold. The 777X is delivering from 2027 [BX-0550]. MAX 7/10 certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299]. The 777X cash is positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so fps is fundable from 2029 and a 2030 launch is not early. Debt repair is on the path I set in July 2026 (about two years, launch around 2029-30) [BG-0068, BX-1305, B-2327]. The developments that had to finish first are done [B-2326, B-2276]. The lift is final only if Malave's buffer and fundable tests and Pope's readiness results come back clean.
H2: cannot bind. The earliest fps EIS is 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year.

H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1). My provisional ruling: held for Round 1, on a re-founded ground. Its literal 2026 ground, the 777X first, has lapsed. Its principle has not: one major development at a time, with the next one feathering in only as the last rolls off [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393]; finish what is in hand before what's next [B-2326]; doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]. From 2030 the program in hand is the fps. Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336]. Any value forgone is logged as a hard-rule cost, not a premium. H3, second half: no 787 Re-engine, ever, once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine.
H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine. launch_7yr with re787 (5 years) is struck.
H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine. Re-baseline once instead [BX-1251, BX-1321].
H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus, and none under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem [BX-1259, BX-1322].
H7: no trigger on this board. If a brief ever reports certification trouble, I treat it as a failed FAA-process gate and launch no fps that round [BX-1309].
H8: plans within epsilon ($1B) are ties that doctrine decides. Doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2B. Every premium is logged.
frame.asks_cfo:
Jay, you are my independent check on these estimates [BX-1316]. Please test them as you tested the 777X baseline: with buffer built in, so we can meet it and maybe beat it [BX-0553].

1. Buffer test (slip leg), with numbers. Each candidate row's S5 against Do Nothing's -3.64 (floor -5.64): B -0.78, C -0.83, E -1.52, F +1.42, H -18.83. Confirm that B and C pass and H fails. Say whether you would veto anything.
2. Fundable when the 777X turns. Confirm that fps is fundable from 2029 [BX-0547] and that a 2030 launch passes. Give me the cash timing of each bill:
   - 10-year $60.32B, booked at EIS 2040;
   - 7-year $65.00B at 2037;
   - via Embraer $100B at 2040;
   - Re-engine $5B at 2035;
   - Rate Increase $2.94B in 2032.
   Show how the real spend spreads over the development years. Confirm that we fund it from operations and debt capacity, with no new equity, and that we stay solidly investment grade on the path [BX-1305, BX-0556]. The Board will not pass anything that leans on equity or puts the rating at risk.
3. Debt penalty. Confirm it is already netted in every grid row, so we do not subtract it twice. Give the discounted penalty by plan. dashboard_game.md §2 shows 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B and via Embraer $52.5B undiscounted, and my card carries 16.3 / 21.7. Tell me which set is right. Is the 10-year ramp the less-debt plan?
4. Ramp. B against C: 10-year ahead by 1.30 in S1 and S3, behind by 0.46 in S2 and S4, ahead by 0.05 in S5. Which carries the more honest buffer? What conservative EIS and risk-case range would you publish at launch so we reset once, not serially [BX-1318, BX-0548]?
5. Re-engine (row F). Confirm the 2-year strain overlap with the 10-year fps and its strain cost, and the item value of -3.58 in S3 and S4. Give your view on a second program alongside the fps while we are still deleveraging.
6. Rate Increase. Confirm the -0.74 item value with fps launched and its 2032 cash cost.
7. Embraer. Anything outside the grid (risk transfer, capital) that would narrow a $13.75B-plus gap? I expect not.

Board risks to keep in view: the Board wants your buffer numbers and your fundable result in writing, and it vetoes via Embraer, any plan below -5.64 in S5, and any plan carrying your standing veto.
frame.asks_ops:
Stephanie, your seat is played by the [NOW] operations doctrine. Please give me results, not adjectives: the Board will not pass a launch or a Rate Increase without your readiness results.

1. KPI status. Is any quality, FAA or supply-chain problem live in 2030? Have the 737 and 787 lines held 2-3 stable months at rate, with the KPIs inside control limits [BX-1271, BX-1259, B-2351]? Run your veto check on a Rate Increase. My lean is hold anyway, because it is worth -0.74 beside an fps launch, but I want the check on record.
2. Boeing-ready. Confirm that the MAX 7/10 are certified and delivering and that the 777X is delivering. I am assuming 2026 and 2027 [BX-1873, BX-0550], with no certification trouble open.
3. Two-front strain and engineering capacity. Can we carry the fps alone with headroom on each ramp? Which ramp lets the plan absorb hiccups, the way the 2024 restart did [BX-1275, B-2295]? What does adding the 787 Re-engine do to engineering capacity? It runs side by side with the fps in 2030-35 even where the board counts only 2 years of overlap. Confirm the fps plan has no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263].
4. Suppliers. With Spirit inside [BG-0064], is the supply base ready for an fps ramp while the 737 runs at rate? Which suppliers need funding to stay hot? How exposed are we to an unattributed bottleneck or loss of engineering talent around EIS, which is the risk case S5?
5. Engines. Can CFM support our rates, Airbus's rates and an fps by 2040 (2037 on the 7-year ramp) [BX-1264, BX-1325]? Give durability lessons for the new engine [BX-1298]. Confirm code 3 as the request and how you would judge another maker's readiness by EIS.
6. Solo or via Embraer. On IP [BX-1330], does Embraer add capital or capacity we lack, or take IP we should keep? The grid prices the Embraer route $13.75B-plus below Do Nothing.

Board risks: a launch your memo fails on KPIs, suppliers or strain, without your veto check showing it resolved, will be vetoed. So will a Rate Increase under any live problem.
frame.initial_lean:
Orders I lean to:
- fps: launch_10yr;
- fps_engine_code: 3 (CFM);
- rate_737: hold;
- re787: hold.
That is one Solo launch, standing alone.

Why:
- It beats Do Nothing by $2.86-4.30B in every column. That passes debt-first and doing less, better.
- It sits 4.86 above Malave's S5 floor, and the risk case (-0.78) is slightly better than the 7-year's (-0.83).
- The fps is fundable now that the 777X has turned [BX-0547].

Expected column (provisional): S4, NGSA plus an A350 Re-engine, with S2 a close second. This is doctrine's reading of Airbus (profile §7), not my record; my confidence on Airbus is low. The lean is the same in S2 and S4, and that is the point: it does not hang on guessing Airbus [B-2313].

On the ramp:
- In S2 and S4 the 7-year is 0.46 ahead, inside epsilon.
- The tie goes to the plan with less to execute and more headroom. That is the 10-year: about $4.7B smaller bill, lower debt penalty, "right than fast" [BX-1241, BX-1275, BX-0548]. It is also 1.30 ahead if Airbus holds or only re-engines the A350.
- I log a soft premium of 0.46 in S2 and S4, and none in S1, S3 or S5.
- I am not choosing either ramp because of NGSA's date.
- I note honestly that the 7-year, by entering service with a 2030 NGSA, would hold incumbency in the NGSA columns where the 10-year dips below 40% for a few years. It also has the Board's higher worst column. If Malave and Pope show the 7-year carries the same buffer and strain headroom, I will weigh it in the decide step.

Rate Increase: hold. It is worth -0.74 beside any fps launch, and fps beats it alone in every column. No premium, and no Airbus in the reasoning.

787 Re-engine: hold under my H3 ruling. One development at a time; bring it back in 2035 only if the A350 has not re-engined and the overlap is within H4. The cost is a hard-rule cost: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, and nil in S3 and S4, where the Re-engine would lose 3.58.

Via Embraer: rejected.

H1: lifted, subject to both memos.

Public line: no fps date before launch. At launch, a conservative EIS with the nominal and risk-case range; no blame on the FAA, suppliers or Airbus. We're turning it; I don't think it's turned.

tests.name: Buffer test (slip leg), plan B: fps launch_10yr + rate_737 hold + re787 hold
tests.threshold: Risk-case column S5 (NGSA + Airbus Delay Tactics) must be no more than $2B below Do Nothing in the same column. Do Nothing S5 is -3.64, so the floor is -5.64. Run as the baseline, not as a sensitivity.
tests.numbers: Row 'fps 10-yr + 787: hold', column S5 = -0.78. Against Do Nothing (-3.64) that is +2.86, and 4.86 above the -5.64 floor. Full row S1-S5: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. Worst column is S4 at -1.96, against Do Nothing's worst of -6.26.

tests.name: Buffer test (slip leg), plan C: fps launch_7yr + rate_737 hold + re787 hold
tests.threshold: S5 no more than $2B below Do Nothing's -3.64 (floor -5.64).
tests.numbers: Row 'fps 7-yr + 787: hold', column S5 = -0.83. Against Do Nothing that is +2.81, and 4.81 above the floor. Full row: +2.20 / +1.12 / -0.42 / -1.50 / -0.83. Worst column is S4 at -1.50.

tests.name: Buffer test (slip leg), every other row without Embraer (plans D, E, F, G, I and the rate/Re-engine combinations)
tests.threshold: S5 at or above -5.64.
tests.numbers: S5 values, with the gap to Do Nothing in brackets: E 'fps 10-yr + 737 rate up' -1.52 (+2.12); 'fps 7-yr + 737 rate up' -1.57 (+2.07); F 'fps 10-yr + 787 Re-engine' +1.42 (+5.06); G 'fps 7-yr + 787 Re-engine' +0.45 (+4.09); 'fps 10-yr + rate + Re-engine' +0.68 (+4.32); 'fps 7-yr + rate + Re-engine' -0.30 (+3.34); D 'hold + rate' -4.38 (-0.74); I 'hold + Re-engine' -0.34 (+3.30); 'hold + rate + Re-engine' -1.08 (+2.56). All clear the floor, so my veto does not reach them and my objections to them are advice only.

tests.name: Buffer test (slip leg), plan H: every fps launch_via_embraer row
tests.threshold: S5 at or above -5.64.
tests.numbers: S5 values, with the gap to Do Nothing in brackets: 'via Embraer + 787: hold' -18.83 (-15.19); '+ 787 Re-engine' -17.47 (-13.83); '+ 737 rate up' -19.58 (-15.94); '+ rate + Re-engine' -18.21 (-14.57). That is 11.83 to 13.94 below the floor. Under the team rule this is my binding veto.

tests.name: Fundable when the 777X turns (Board gate; ask 2)
tests.threshold: fps is fundable once the 777X is cash-positive (from 2029). A 2030 launch passes unless the brief shows otherwise. Fund it from operations and debt capacity, with no new equity (inference).
tests.numbers: 777X cash is near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], with first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550]. Launch year 2030 is not before 2029. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. Funding, assuming an even spread over development (inference; the board books the bill at EIS): 10-yr about $6.03B a year over 2030-39, against the brief's airplane operating profit of $6.7B a year (90%); 7-yr about $9.29B a year over 2030-36 (139%, so about $2.6B a year borrowed); via Embraer about $10.0B a year. On the 10-year ramp there is no new equity: operations plus debt capacity, since tax, interest and sustaining capex leave it tight. The board does not model the rating. It books each full bill as debt at EIS, taking debt/EV from 35% ($45B on $130B) to 81% (10-yr), 85% (7-yr) or 112% (Embraer), and the netted penalty is its price for that. I can support the investment-grade rating on the 10-year phasing standing alone, but not with a second bill running in the same years. Condition: barring a 777X cash path that missed my 2025 guide, or a sustained fall in 737/787 deliveries or margins.

tests.name: Balance sheet first: debt penalty (ask 3)
tests.threshold: Grid ΔPV already nets each plan's discounted penalty (α 0.30 × debt × (debt/EV)²), so never subtract it again. Between plans within ε ($1B) on the expected column, prefer the one that adds the smaller penalty (inference).
tests.numbers: The penalty is netted in every grid row (rules payoff; dashboard_game.md §2). The right set is dashboard_game.md §2: undiscounted 10-yr $19.1B, 7-yr $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine alone $0.6B. These reproduce from the formula on $45B of debt and a $130B EV. For example, (45+60.32) × 0.30 × (105.32/130)² = 20.74, less 1.62 today, gives 19.1. The 16.3/21.7 set fits older bills of $55.25B/$64.47B (my own card carries them too), so it is stale. Discounted at 10.5% to 2026 at EIS (my arithmetic, not a grid figure): 10-yr about $4.7B (2040), 7-yr about $7.3B (2037), via Embraer about $13.0B (2040), Re-engine alone about $0.24B (2035), Rate Increase alone about $0.19B (2032). These are not additive for combined plans. The 10-year is the less-debt plan: its bill is $4.68B smaller, its penalty $2.9B smaller undiscounted (about $2.6B discounted), and it lands three years later. In the expected column S4, B (-1.96) and C (-1.50) sit within ε, so this test prefers B.

tests.name: Meet and beat: ramp, launch_10yr (B) against launch_7yr (C) (ask 4)
tests.threshold: Among plans within ε ($1B) on the expected column, prefer the one with the higher worst column (inference).
tests.numbers: Advice, not a veto. The expected column is S4 on Ortberg's provisional read; I have no Airbus evidence of my own. In S4, C scores -1.50 and B -1.96, 0.46 apart and inside ε. Worst columns are C -1.50 and B -1.96, so the rule prefers the 7-year by 0.46. B minus C by column: +1.30 / -0.46 / +1.30 / -0.46 / +0.05. B never trails C by more than 0.46, while C trails B by 1.30 in S1 and S3. Mean of the five columns: B +0.46, C +0.11. I set the rule aside on balance sheet first and log 0.46 as a premium. On the honest buffer: the 10-year is the schedule baseline with room in it. At launch, publish entry into service in 2040, no earlier. State the risk case as a condition: S5, 5 pp of share lost for five years from EIS, -0.78 on the grid. Hold any earlier internal date back as upside. On the 7-year, publishing 2037 means a nominal date with no buffer: the 777X lesson [BX-0550] (inference).

tests.name: Cash path of each bill (ask 2)
tests.threshold: When each bill lands, and whether two land together (heavy use, then neutral, then positive) [BX-0547].
tests.numbers: Board bookings, nominal (with PV at 10.5% to 2026 in brackets): Rate Increase $2.94B in 2032 ($1.62B); Re-engine $5B in 2035 ($2.04B); 7-yr $65.00B in 2037 ($21.67B); 10-yr $60.32B in 2040 ($14.91B); via Embraer $100B in 2040 ($24.71B). Real spend if spread evenly (inference; real programmes are heaviest mid-development): 10-yr about $6.0B a year over 2030-39; 7-yr about $9.3B a year over 2030-36; via Embraer about $10.0B a year over 2030-39; Re-engine about $1.0B a year over 2030-34; the Rate Increase in 2030-32. Plan B carries one bill, in 2040: heavy use through the 2030s, then neutral and positive after EIS, as on the 777X. In no candidate do two bills land in the same year. But in F the fps and Re-engine spend run side by side in 2030-34, about $7.0B a year against $6.7B of operating profit, and in G about $10.3B a year.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip or cancel
tests.threshold: Cancel write-off = bill × years elapsed ÷ development years, and the debt penalty stays. H5: never cancel. Cost any slip once, in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost).
tests.numbers: No cancel is in play. For scale, a cancel in 2035 would write off $30.16B on the 10-yr (60.32 × 5/10) or $46.43B on the 7-yr (65.00 × 5/7), plus the penalty. By 2035 the 7-year has sunk 71% of its bill and the 10-year 50%. A Boeing EIS slip is not on the board; S5 prices only a 5 pp share loss for five years from EIS. A real slip adds concessions, rework, learning curve and carrying cost [B-2349], and the 10-year ramp has more room to absorb one. Reset once, not serially.

tests.name: Rate step: 737 Rate Increase (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA [BX-0554]. On the board, $2.94B in 2032 buys +5 pp in 2032-36 (every year only if no new narrowbody is ever launched). It must add value.
tests.numbers: Advice, not a veto: the KPI gate is Pope's seat. Gate: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Value with fps launched is -0.74 in every column: B 3.50 / 0.66 / 0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78 becomes E 2.76 / -0.08 / 0.14 / -2.70 / -1.52, and C becomes 1.46 / 0.38 / -1.17 / -2.25 / -1.57. With fps on hold it is +2.30 in S1 and S3 and -0.74 in S2, S4 and S5. Cash is $2.94B in 2032 (PV $1.62B), with a formula penalty of about $0.34B undiscounted. 2030 is the only round it is offered, so declining is final. Hold.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine beside fps: strain and downside (ask 5)
tests.threshold: Count the $5B bill at EIS and any strain overlap with fps as cost. H4 allows at most 2 years of overlap. Advice only, unless the plan fails the buffer test.
tests.numbers: Advice, not a veto. On the board's measure, fps development runs EIS-7 to EIS (2033-40 on the 10-yr) and the Re-engine runs 2030-35, so they overlap 2 years. Strain is $3B × 2/5 = $1.2B undiscounted, already netted. With the 7-yr (2030-37) the overlap is 5 years and $3.0B, which breaches H4. Item value against B: +2.20 / +2.20 / -3.58 / -3.58 / +2.20; against C: +1.27 / +1.27 / -4.51 / -4.51 / +1.28. Row F passes my buffer test (S5 +1.42), so I have no veto. But a second programme while we deleverage adds about $1.0B a year in 2030-34 on top of about $6.0B a year of fps spend, and -3.58 in two plausible columns is a downside I would not take. Hold; revisit in 2035 only if the A350 has not re-engined and the overlap is within H4.

tests.name: via Embraer outside the grid (ask 7)
tests.threshold: Anything off the grid (risk transfer, partner capital) would have to close a gap of $13.75B or more to Do Nothing, and $15.19B in S5.
tests.numbers: The board books $100B to Boeing in 2040 with a $52.5B undiscounted penalty, against $60.32B and $19.1B for the Solo 10-yr with the same 2040 EIS. That is $39.68B more bill and $33.4B more penalty, or about $9.80B + $8.24B = $18.04B in PV. This matches the grid gap to B in S1 (-14.55 against +3.50 = 18.05). The board prices no partner capital or risk transfer, so nothing narrows the gap. It fails my buffer test and the balance sheet.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8)
tests.threshold: Report every doctrine or objective premium in $B; the total stays within $2B. Name the condition that would break the number.
tests.numbers: Measured on my recommendation (B) against the best plan that respects the hard rules and the Board's tests (Solo rows with no Re-engine or Rate Increase): S1 0 (B best at +3.50); S2 0.46 (C +1.12 against B +0.66); S3 0 (B +0.88); S4 0.46 (C -1.50 against B -1.96); S5 0 (B -0.78 against C -0.83). The doctrine premium is 0.46 in the expected column S4, on the grounds of balance sheet first [BX-0556] and schedule buffer [BX-0553], well within $2B. No objective premium: no plan reaches 50% by 2040. I note that on Ortberg's read the 10-yr dips below 40% for a few years in S2 and S4, where C holds incumbency at no cost; taking C for that objective would cost 1.30 in S1 and S3. Re-engine value forgone under H3 is a hard-rule cost, not a premium: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, nil in S3 and S4. Condition: the premium holds barring an fps schedule slip, which the board does not price.

vetoes.plan: Any plan with fps: launch_via_embraer (all four rows: with holds, + 787 Re-engine, + 737 rate up, + both)
vetoes.ground: Buffer test (slip leg). In S5 (risk case, NGSA + Delay Tactics) the four rows score -18.83, -17.47, -19.58 and -18.21. Against Do Nothing's -3.64 that is -15.19, -13.83, -15.94 and -14.57, all below the -5.64 floor by 11.83 to 13.94. The team rule (teams.md §9) makes this binding; the CEO must revise within it.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch in Round 1 (beside either fps ramp, or alone)
vetoes.ground: Advice only. Every Re-engine row passes my buffer test (F S5 +1.42), so I have no veto. But its item value is -3.58 in S3 and S4 with the 10-yr (-4.51 with the 7-yr, which also breaches H4 at a 5-year overlap). It adds about $1.0B a year of spend in 2030-34 on top of about $6.0B a year of fps while we deleverage, and its $5B bill lands in 2035.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase beside any fps launch
vetoes.ground: Advice only. The item value is -0.74 in every column (e.g. B 3.50 becomes 2.76 in S1, and -0.78 becomes -1.52 in S5), and it costs $2.94B in 2032. It passes my buffer test, so I have no veto; the KPI gate is Pope's.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Toward the 7-year ramp: Pope's results show it carries the same strain and supplier headroom as the 10-year, and its roughly $9.3B a year can be phased without borrowing above airplane operating profit. Or the ExCo firms the expected column at S2 or S4 and weighs the higher floor (-1.50 against -1.96) and incumbency. It passes my buffer test by 2.81, so I would accept it. Toward hold: Pope reports a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem; the 777X has not turned cash-positive; or a grid shows either Solo ramp below -5.64 in S5. On the Re-engine: only in a later round, with the A350 Re-engine off the table and the overlap within H4. On Embraer: only a grid row within $2B of Do Nothing in S5. No off-grid capital transfer can produce that on this board.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran your grid the way we ran the 777X baseline: the risk case is the baseline, not a sensitivity.

Buffer test. Do Nothing scores -3.64 in S5, so the floor is -5.64. The 10-year ramp scores -0.78 and the 7-year -0.83: both pass with about $2.8B to spare. Every Embraer row fails, at -17.47 to -19.58, at least $13.8B below Do Nothing. Under the team rule that is my binding veto. Nothing else fails it.

Fundable. The 777X is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so a 2030 launch passes.

Cash path. The board books $60.32B in 2040 for the 10-year ramp and $65.00B in 2037 for the 7-year, with penalties of $19.1B and $22.0B undiscounted, already netted. Phased over development, that is about $6.0B a year against $6.7B of airplane operating profit, or about $9.3B a year, which we would borrow to cover.

Ramp. The 7-year has the higher worst column and leads by 0.46 in S2 and S4, inside $1B; the 10-year leads by 1.30 in S1 and S3. Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet comes first [BX-0556]. I recommend launch_10yr with code 3, and log 0.46 as premium. I would not veto the 7-year.

Hold the Rate Increase (-0.74 in every column) and the Re-engine (-3.58 in S3 and S4).

At launch, publish entry into service in 2040, barring a supply-chain or talent disruption around EIS, and hold any earlier date as upside. That baseline we can meet and potentially beat.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can the plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S5 (NGSA plus Delay Tactics) against Do Nothing, and state how much of the plan's value depends on the nominal date. A plan passes if it keeps a positive item value in S5 and stays above the -5.64 floor.
tests.numbers: 10-year Solo: S5 -0.78, which is +2.86 against Do Nothing (-3.64) and 4.86 above the floor. $1.44B is lost from S2 (+0.66) to S5 (-0.78), or 33% of its S2 item value of +4.30. 7-year Solo: S5 -0.83 (+2.81 against Do Nothing). It loses $1.95B from S2 (+1.12) to S5, or 41% of its +4.76. Doctrine's slip prior for a clean sheet (profile.md §3, inference) is a central +3 years (range +2 to +5). A 7-year ramp launched in 2030 slips under it from 2037 to 2040, the 10-year ramp's nominal date. The 10-year therefore publishes a date we can keep. Via Embraer: S5 -18.83, which is 13.19 below the floor. It fails.

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity (doctrine)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers: Recommended plan (fps alone, re787 hold): 0 years of overlap and $0 of strain on either ramp. Reference rows: (a) 10-year plus Re-engine. The fps counts 2033-40 and the Re-engine 2030-35, so the overlap is 2 years (2033-35) and the strain $1.2B undiscounted. That sits at the H4 limit on the board, but on the real calendar both programmes are in development side by side for 2030-35, which is against one development at a time [B-0341]. The Re-engine item falls from +3.30 (fps hold, S1) to +2.20 beside the 10-year, so 1.10 of strain and extra debt is netted in. (b) 7-year plus Re-engine: 5 years of overlap (2030-35) and $3.0B of strain. This fails H4.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers: 10-year: EIS 2040, strain 0. The $60.32B bill spreads to about $6.03B a year over 2030-40 (linear, as the rules' cancel write-off implies; inference). 7-year: EIS 2037, strain 0. Its $65.00B is about $9.29B a year over 2030-37, a 54% heavier annual engineering and cash load. Both can be delivered standing alone. The 10-year carries the headroom to absorb hiccups the way the 2024 restart was planned [BX-1275, B-2295]: its nominal date equals the 7-year ramp's date under the central slip. Grid: the 10-year is ahead by 1.30 in S1 and S3 and by 0.05 in S5; the 7-year is ahead by 0.46 in S2 and S4 (inside epsilon) and has the higher worst column (-1.50 against -1.96). My advice is the 10-year. The 7-year also passes every test of mine.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied by inference)
tests.threshold: Solo fps where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Go via Embraer only if the partner adds capital or capacity Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: Solo passes; via Embraer fails. Embraer adds no capacity: the same 2040 EIS as the 10-year ramp, and no strain to halve because no second programme runs. It adds no capital either. Boeing's bill is $100B against $60.32B (+$39.68B), and the undiscounted debt penalty is $52.5B against $19.1B. The Embraer item value is -14.55 / -13.75 / -14.56 / -13.75 / -15.19 (S1-S5), and the route shares airframe IP we should keep.

tests.name: KPI gate for the 737 Rate Increase: my veto (doctrine)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, at least 6 months apart, KPI-gated. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: The 2030 brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. On the board, the 737 and 787 delivered steadily: 800 NB (40.0%) and 100 WB (58.8%) a year, flat 2026-29. The board carries no KPI data: the 2-3 stable months at rate [BX-1271] and 47 a month cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069] are company record passed by the CEO, not my record and not in the brief. A step ordered now lands in 2032, well over 6 months after any prior step. The gate passes, so the KPI veto is not invoked and does not bind. Supplier caveat (doctrine): beyond 47 the supply chain binds [B-2340], and an fps ramp would load the same base.

tests.name: Supplier readiness for the fps ramp (doctrine)
tests.threshold: No live supply-chain problem; fragile suppliers kept funded and hot; the plan survives the risk case (unattributed bottleneck or talent poaching) with value above Do Nothing.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no supply-chain problem in 2030. Spirit inside since December 2025 [BG-0064] is company record via the CEO, not mine. The brief names no fragile supplier, so I name none. Doctrine: keep fragile suppliers above Boeing's rate and funded [B-2330, BX-1243, B-2264], with cost-plus or back-to-back terms. The risk case S5 costs 5 pp for 5 years from fps EIS: $1.44B (10-year) and $1.95B (7-year) against S2, with item value still +2.86 / +2.81. Our answer to a bottleneck: embed staff, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire. Never cancel (H5), and attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure.

tests.name: Boeing-ready: MAX 7/10, 777X, no production-certification concurrency (doctrine; company record via CEO)
tests.threshold: MAX 7/10 certified and delivering; 777X delivering; no certification trouble open (teams.md §9: treat as done unless a certification inject is live). The fps plan builds no production airplanes before certification.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no certification or FAA problem in 2030. MAX 7/10 certification in 2026 [BX-1873] and the 777X first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550] are not in the brief. I accept them under the §9 script. They are company record, not mine. No production-certification concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]: neither ramp requires it on the board. It is a plan requirement, and the 10-year ramp leaves the more room to certify before building at rate.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: 737 Rate Increase (inference from one remark [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it, in the expected column.
tests.numbers: This result applies to the Rate Increase only; the recommended plan holds the rate. With fps launched it is -0.74 in every column on either ramp (10-year 2.76 against 3.50; 7-year 1.46 against 2.20). With fps on hold it is +2.30 in S1 and S3 and -0.74 in S2, S4 and S5. The CEO's expected column is S4 (S2 close), so the item is -0.74 there. Cost $2.94B in 2032. It does not earn the capacity: hold.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332], applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number, with a sensitivity per unit of change.
tests.numbers: 10-year: $60.32B booked at EIS 2040 (about $6.03B a year over 2030-40); undiscounted debt penalty $19.1B. 7-year: $65.00B at 2037 (about $9.29B a year); $22.0B. Via Embraer: $100B at 2040 (about $10.0B a year); $52.5B. Re-engine: $5B at 2035 (about $1.0B a year over 2030-35); $0.6B alone. Rate Increase: $2.94B in 2032. Sensitivity: each year of EIS pulled forward costs about $1.56B of bill ($4.68B over 3 years) and about $1.0B of undiscounted penalty ($2.9B over 3 years). Debt is $45B on an EV of $130B. Penalty and strain are already netted in the grid, so do not subtract them twice. The 10-year Solo is the best cash conversion of the launches. Malave's veto decides the slip leg.

tests.name: Engine readiness by fps EIS (doctrine; not a payoff item)
tests.threshold: The requested maker has a new NB engine ready by fps EIS. CFM is always available.
tests.numbers: Code 3 (CFM) is always available by EIS, as a LEAP derivative at worst. If NGSA also takes code 3, the later airframe moves to code 7, with no payoff change. Another maker counts only with a public engine-ready date on or before EIS: GTF2 6 years after launch, UltraFan NB 7, the Joint Venture 6 after forming. Rounds fall in 2030 and 2035, so only a 2030 engine launch makes 2037. A 2035 launch is ready 2041-42 and misses even 2040, unless a Joint Venture folds in a further-along solo programme. Durability: require a matured engine before EIS [BX-1298, BX-1325]. CFM's load across both airframers' rates [BX-1264] is not on the board.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (any combination)
vetoes.ground: KPI veto checked and NOT invoked. The 2030 brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so the team rule's KPI veto does not bind. Advice only: the item is -0.74 in every column beside an fps launch, and -0.74 in the expected S4 even with fps on hold. Beyond 47 the supply chain binds [B-2340]. H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_7yr + re787 launch (option G)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag, H4: 5 years of overlap (fps 2030-37, Re-engine 2030-35) against the 2-year limit, with $3.0B of strain undiscounted. This is not my veto; the rule binds the CEO.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_10yr + re787 launch (option F)
vetoes.ground: Advice: at the H4 limit on the board (2 years, 2033-35, $1.2B of strain), but on the real calendar the two programmes are in development side by side for 2030-35. Doctrine allows one development at a time [B-0341, B-1393]. The Re-engine item is -3.58 in S3 and S4. Hold under the CEO's H3 ruling.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_via_embraer (option H)
vetoes.ground: Advice (IP test): it gives up airframe IP and adds neither capacity nor capital. The bill is +$39.68B for the same 2040 EIS, and S5 is -18.83 against the -5.64 floor.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Four things would change my view. (1) A brief that reports a live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. I would then invoke the binding KPI veto on any Rate Increase, and under the CEO's H7 line support no fps launch that round. (2) A supplier and workforce plan showing the 7-year ramp can hold 2037 with the same headroom as the 10-year, that is, absorb a 2-3 year slip. I would then rate the ramps a tie on delivery and let the 0.46 in S2/S4 and the Board's higher worst column (-1.50 against -1.96) decide. (3) A partner that brings capital or capacity Boeing lacks at a Boeing bill at or below the Solo $60.32B. (4) With fps on hold and an expected column of S1 or S3, the Rate Increase earns +2.30, and stable KPIs would let me back it.
ops.memo:
My record is thin: two Global Services events, nothing from BCA. Delivery, IP and cash tests are my record, applied to airplanes by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time, predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, with 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies a year, flat over 2026-29. The KPI gate passes, so my veto does not bind. Both Solo ramps pass. In the risk case the 10-year stays $2.86B above Do Nothing and the 7-year $2.81B. The 10-year has less riding on its nominal date: it loses $1.44B from S2 to S5, against $1.95B. Its 2040 date is also where doctrine's central three-year clean-sheet slip would put a 7-year ramp.

Second, engineering capacity. The fps alone has zero overlap and zero strain on either ramp. A 787 Re-engine counts 2 years ($1.2B) on the board, but it runs beside the fps for 2030-35. One development at a time: hold.

Third, cash. Each year of EIS pulled forward costs about $1.56B of bill and $1B of undiscounted debt penalty: $9.29B a year on the 7-year against $6.03B on the 10-year.

And finally, IP. The airframe is ours. Embraer adds $39.68B of bill for the same 2040 EIS. Solo.

The Rate Increase is worth -0.74 in every column beside a launch. Hold.

Orders: launch_10yr, code 3, rate hold, Re-engine hold. The 7-year also passes every test of mine.

decision.public_statement:
When I started, I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We've spent these years earning that. The 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are delivering. Our production lines are stable on the KPIs. Our balance sheet is healthier. I think we've turned this ship. I don't think the work is done.

Today we are launching a new single-aisle airplane. It is a Boeing airplane, and we will own the design. We are taking the ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. That is a planning date with headroom built in, not a stretch target. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We have tested the plan against a harder case, including disruption in the supply chain or our engineering workforce around entry into service, and it still stands. If the schedule moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

A few things will not change. We will certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll share risk with our suppliers on terms that work for both of us, and we'll keep the supply chain funded and healthy. We'll fund this from our operations and our debt capacity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

We are not changing production rates today. The 737 stays where its KPIs have it, and we are not starting a second development alongside this one. Doing less, and doing it better, is what got us here.

This decision rests on our own readiness, not on anyone else's timeline. The financials will follow our production performance. We have a lot of work in front of us, and we're going to do it one step at a time.
decision.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 1 (2030), team rule of teams.md §9: I propose and decide; Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can block.

1. Vetoes in force. Malave holds one binding veto: every fps launch_via_embraer row fails his slip leg. In S5 they score -18.83, -17.47, -19.58 and -18.21, against a floor of -5.64 (Do Nothing -3.64). Embraer is out and I do not contest it. Pope ran the KPI check on a Rate Increase and did not invoke her veto: the brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's H4 flag on fps 7-yr + Re-engine (5 years of overlap) is correct; that row is struck. Neither colleague vetoes the 10-year Solo, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live problem, with 800 narrowbody and 100 widebody deliveries a year, flat over 2026-29. 47 a month cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069] is company record, not in the brief.
- Market, technology and Boeing ready?
  - Market: waiting is not free. Do Nothing scores -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 if Airbus moves.
  - Technology: H2 cannot bind; EIS 2040 is well after 2035.
  - Boeing: see the H1 ruling below.
- If certification takes longer? Read S5 first. The 10-year scores -0.78 there, +2.86 against Do Nothing and 4.86 above the floor.
- Doing less, better? The 10-year Solo beats Do Nothing by +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86 in S1-S5, so it is above ε in every column. It carries the smallest bill of the launches.

3. H1 ruling (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were unfinished developments and unrepaired debt [B-2326, BX-1305], and they no longer hold:
- the 777X is delivering from 2027 [BX-0550];
- the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299];
- 777X cash was near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes for a 2030 launch;
- debt repair ran on the path I set at Farnborough, about two more years with a launch around 2029-30 [BG-0068, B-2327];
- Spirit is inside [BG-0064].
The post-2025 outcomes rest on the teams.md §9 script and Board-file record, not on my own words, and the brief reports no certification trouble. My FAA-process gate [BX-1309] therefore passes.

4. H3 ruling, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): held on a re-founded ground. The literal 2026 ground (the 777X first) has lapsed. The principle has not: one major development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], finish what is in hand first [B-2326], do less and do it better [BX-1239]. From 2030 the program in hand is the fps. The Board's Downside test also bars the Re-engine: -3.58 in S3 and S4 beside the 10-year. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written.

5. The ramp, my main call. In my expected column S4 (doctrine's reading of Airbus, profile §7; my own confidence on Airbus is Low), C (7-year) scores -1.50 and B (10-year) -1.96. That is 0.46 apart, inside ε, so doctrine breaks the tie. I take the 10-year:
- Doing less [BX-1239]: the bill is $4.68B smaller ($60.32B against $65.00B). The undiscounted debt penalty is $2.9B lower ($19.1B against $22.0B; Malave confirms the 16.3/21.7 set on my card is stale), about $2.6B lower discounted.
- Headroom [BX-1275, B-2295, BX-1241]: about $6.0B a year of spend against about $9.3B. The 7-year would need about $2.6B a year borrowed above airplane operating profit. Malave supports the rating only on the 10-year phasing.
- Honest date: Pope's clean-sheet slip prior (central +3 years, doctrine) puts a 7-year launch at 2040 anyway. So 2040 is a date we can meet and maybe beat [BX-0553].
- Robustness: B leads C by 1.30 in S1 and S3 and by 0.05 in S5, and trails by only 0.46 in S2 and S4. Its five-column mean is +0.46 against +0.11.
- Airbus does not set the date [B-2313]. The 7-year's one structural edge is entering service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched in 2030. Choosing it for that edge would time our airplane to theirs, which I will not do.
I log 0.46 as a doctrine premium, within the $2B cap. The Board recommended the 7-year for its higher worst column. I take that seriously, but the 10-year's worst column (-1.96) is still $4.30B above Do Nothing's in the same column. Doctrine (profile §11.4) tilts the same way as my record here.

6. Rate Increase: hold. Beside any fps launch its item value is -0.74 in every column (B 3.50 / 0.66 / 0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78 becomes 2.76 / -0.08 / 0.14 / -2.70 / -1.52). It fails the value condition and the Board's business case. Declining in 2030 is final, but it costs nothing in any column beside the fps. Airbus played no part in this reasoning (H6).

7. Embraer: out on Malave's binding veto and Pope's IP test. It costs $39.68B more bill for the same 2040 EIS.

8. Board items and rows.
- fps launch_10yr (with code 3 riding with it). Submitted row: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. With the item at its default (Do Nothing): 0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. Item value: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. It is above $1B in the expected column, never below -$1B, and S5 clears the floor by 4.86.
- No other Board item: the rate and the Re-engine are held.
- Premium 0.46 (S4, doctrine). Hard-rule cost from H3: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, nil in S3 and S4.

Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice: the expected column (profile §7); the re-founded H3 ground (company record on one development at a time); engine code 3 (Low on my record; doctrine and inference); the supplier-readiness and strain tests (Pope's seat is doctrine-played).

recommendations.text: Correct the Re-engine window, including our own guidance. On the 10-year ramp the fps counts 2033-40 (EIS - 7 to EIS). A 787 Re-engine launched in 2035 would count 2035-40: 5 years of overlap against the 2-year limit (H4 and our One development test). The 2035 window that both our guidance and the decision named is therefore closed by arithmetic. The earliest window is the 2045 round, after fps EIS, and only if Airbus has not re-engined the A350 (H3, second half). Please plan widebody growth on Charleston capacity until then.

Report funding and the rating path to the Finance Committee every year. Malave's even spread is about $6.0B a year against $6.7B of airplane operating profit (90%). He says the peak years will run tighter, and he supports the investment-grade rating only on this phasing standing alone. Bring the actual phasing, the debt path and the rating outlook each round. Any need for new equity, or any threat to investment grade, comes back to this board before it is committed. Debt stays the first call on free cash.

Report safety readiness directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee. Pope noted that the KPI stability she relied on (2-3 stable months, 47 a month cleared) is company record the CEO passed in, not brief data. The Aerospace Safety Committee asks to hear the 737 and 787 KPI, supplier and certification results directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer each round. It also asks for the certify-before-rate commitment (no production-certification concurrency) to be written into the fps programme plan.

The fps is now a core development. Re-baseline it, never cancel it, for a slip, a charge, a supplier problem or Airbus entering service first (H5). If the date moves, reset once and early, cost the slip in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), and bring it to this board. Our Cancellation test protects the programme unless keeping it loses at least $1B in every plausible column.

On the ramp, we accept the reasons given for the 10-year ramp and the 0.46 premium logged in S2 and S4. We will hold management to that row: S4 at -1.96, still $4.30B above Do Nothing. The decision records the incumbency objective as not met, with share dipping below 40% for roughly 2038-43 if Airbus launches NGSA. Report that path honestly each round. Do not answer it by tying any order to Airbus's timing.

Engine code (not a veto ground). Code 3 is acceptable: CFM is always available by 2040. If NGSA, launched earlier, also takes code 3, the fps moves to code 7. Revisit the code in 2035 against the public engine-ready dates. Request only makers whose new engine is ready and matured, with durability shown, before 2040.

Disclosure. We support a public 2040 entry into service with the risk case stated as a condition and any earlier date held back. Keep public claims on KPIs and deliveries to what the company can substantiate. Attribute nothing to the FAA, suppliers or Airbus. Keep a running log of every premium (0.46 this round) and of hard-rule costs (the Re-engine forgone under H3) separately. We will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions, and we judge this choice on the long cycle.

board_review.note: The Board approves fps: launch_10yr, with engine code 3 riding with it. Its item value against Do Nothing is +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86 (S1-S5): above $1B in the expected S4 and never below -$1B. S5 at -0.78 sits 4.86 above the -5.64 floor. The CEO's written H1 ruling cites the 777X, the MAX 7/10, 777X cash from 2029 and debt repair. Malave's buffer and fundable tests and Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results pass, with no ExCo veto standing. The premium of 0.46 is logged within the $2B cap. We recommended the 7-year ramp; the CEO answered with reasons, which is not a veto ground. One correction to our own guidance: on this ramp a 2035 Re-engine would overlap the fps by 5 years, so its earliest window is 2045. We ask for yearly funding and rating reports to Finance, and KPI results direct to Aerospace Safety. The fps is to be re-baselined, never cancelled.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: nobody has launched a new narrowbody yet. When one comes, we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM, together with our partners at Safran, is launching a new ducted engine now. That way a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first. We don't expect it ready before 2036. We'll report against that gate every year, on test, not on slides. It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE. We're all in on that technology, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

CFM is also teaming with Embraer. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, GE is upgrading the GEnx for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: when the airframers move, and what they pick. So we plan on the low case, and we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Do Nothing costs $32.07B (S2) to $105.01B (S6) in every column where an airframer launches. A new NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040. We have no birthright on that order [CX-0564]. We win by having a new CFM engine ready before that entry, offered to every airframer. We don't press anyone into an Open Fan wait, and we keep the payout whole.

DECISION: ducted launch, partner_embraer launch, genx upgrade_genx9, open_fan hold, lobby_emissions hold. This is the best grid plan in S2-S5 (-5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61, S1-S6). Against hold it runs -5.22 / +11.38 / +13.82 / +10.94 / +13.62 / -0.60. Both Ghai and Ali recommend the same orders.

EXPECTED COLUMN: S2. Airbus has the strongest pull on the public rules (an NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year), and code 6 repeats today's dual-sourced A320neo, which is the record, not a hope. The low-case column is S3, and the decision is the same there. Weights are in predictions: S1 0.25, S2 0.30, S3 0.15, S4 0.05, S5 0.15, S6 0.10. I book expected PV at the equal-weight -50.41, below the -38.70 on my weights and well below S2's -20.69 [CX-0248, CX-0536].

EACH BOARD ITEM AGAINST ITS DEFAULT (S1-S6):
- Ducted. Embraer defaults with it, so the default row is GEnx upgrade alone. -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38. Expected S2: +10.61. Worst S1: -6.00, exactly its bill ($4B R&D + $2B strain). Weighted +5.94 on my weights, +6.55 equal; breakeven at an S1 weight of 0.62. Alone against hold: -4.00 / +10.17 / +10.17 / +8.43 / +10.88 / -0.49; weighted +5.58 / +5.86.
- Partner Embraer. Default row is Ducted + GEnx upgrade. 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12. Expected +2.44, worst 0.00; never negative.
- GEnx upgrade. Default row is Ducted + Embraer. +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.77 / +0.78. It runs as the third project, not the second.

HARD RULE 3 TRIGGER (named): S3, where an NGSA on code 2 takes Airbus's whole slot from CFM; also S6 (codes 1 and 2). It is on the grid, not yet on the public record. Ghai passes the Ducted's volumes-first test under this carve-out (+10.17 alone, +13.05 in the package in S3).

THE S1 COST, NAMED [CX-0301, CX-0609]. If nobody moves, the package costs $6.00B against GEnx alone ($5.22B against hold), and the Ducted alone costs $4.00B. That is the whole bill, buying nothing. It is worth it for four reasons:
- Every launch column costs $32-105B under Do Nothing, and the package recovers $10-13B in each of S2-S5.
- The downside is bounded at the bill.
- The weighted value is positive unless S1 carries more than about 62%.
- Timing is now or never for this round's airframes: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036, one year ahead of a 2037 entry, while a 2035 launch is ready only in 2041. A late Ducted still earns from its ready year, but S3 is the slot where being late costs most.

TIE-BREAK. The package and Ducted + Embraer are 0.77-0.78 apart in every column, within epsilon. Safety and quality do not separate them: Ali raises no flag, and the GEnx upgrade is a derivative on a proven lineage. Delivery and cost favour the package: it defends the 787 customer on product [CX-0599, CX-0615] at +0.78 with no added strain. Ghai also vetoes Ducted + Embraer without GEnx. The package beats Ducted alone by more than epsilon in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65).

OPEN FAN AND LOBBY: HOLD. H2 applies: every NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040, before a 2045 Open Fan. Against hold it runs -8.00 / -57.60 / -35.40 / -41.46 / -51.84 / -16.07. Its RISE premium would be $8.78B to $37.34B, above the $15B allowance in five of six columns. A 2030 launch is ready no earlier than a 2035 one. Lobby does nothing without a live Open Fan (-1.00 in every column). RISE stays whole as technology and is never cancelled for cost (H5). The one RISE allowance stays unused, kept for an airframer path [CX-0469, CX-0205].

MY 20% LINE: rebutted, not struck. The line binds the next-generation product, RISE [CX-0217]. Ali confirms a ducted engine gets less than half the open fan's gain [CX-0183, CX-0180], so it will not meet 20%. It is therefore offered and described only as a defensive engine under H3, never as our next generation, and the statement says so in words. Durability is not traded [CX-0208]: Ali raises no safety or durability flag; the Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade against; and durability holds the date, never the reverse. Gate reviews are cross-functional [CX-0012].

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity rule):
- Ducted: consent assumed. A defence that keeps an airframer on CFM fits joint practice in serving both airframers [CX-0185, CX-0587]. Safran shares 50-50 in the installed-base annuity at risk in S3. There is no price talk, and RISE, the joint next generation, is untouched.
- Partner Embraer: consent assumed. A CFM engine for a third airframer serves every airframer and locks no one out. This is inference; there is no Embraer evidence.
- Open Fan and Lobby: held, so nothing to gate.
- GEnx: GE alone, no gate.
- Any CFM price or terms: joint with Safran [CX-0184].

MONEY (Ghai):
- New R&D and strain run $0.67B a year for the Ducted and $1.00B for the package, inside 2-3% of about $44B revenue ($0.88-1.32B).
- Against about $2.55B of room after a 70%+ return of about $8.5B free cash flow [CX-0645], headroom is $1.55B. No debt, no rating effect.
- Premium is $0.00 in S2 and on both sets of weights.

SUPPLY (Ali): the package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65 over the Ducted alone). If the base can carry only one project, the Ducted goes alone.

STANDING COMMITMENT FOR THE BOARD REVIEW: if Partner Embraer is vetoed, GEnx goes with it (-1.22 as the second project), leaving the Ducted alone. If the Ducted is vetoed, Embraer falls and I run GEnx upgrade alone (+0.78).

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove Embraer, Lobby, GEnx as the third project, and the cancel path. My record never addresses Embraer or lobbying (profile §6; dashboard_game §2, §5).

NEXT ROUND: I will look at the airframer launches and selections on the record. If no threat appears by 2035, a cancel writes off $3.33B to save $0.67B, so the decision is judged then on its own grid, never for RISE.

I took all of his binding vetoes as guardrails, and none is ordered: no Open Fan, no Lobby, no GEnx beside a Ducted alone, no S1 expected column, and no Embraer without GEnx. His one failed test on the plan, volumes-first on Partner Embraer, I answered as he proposed. I declared its $0.00 S1 gap inside the package in premium_b and recorded it in overrides. I also took his guide-low advice and booked -50.41. His volume dates slip [CX-0987], and here the unverified volume is the airframer's. memo_weighing.ops: Ali's memo is a thin record. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, and on supply and Embraer he says he is following doctrine and my description of his job [CX-0633]. So I took his date and physics tests as binding and checked his supply view against doctrine. Dates: the Ducted is ready in 2036 as a test-gated floor, the Open Fan not before 2045 whether launched in 2030 or 2035, and the statement gives no RISE demo date and no Ducted date before 2036. Physics: he confirms the Ducted will not reach 20% [CX-0183, CX-0180], which lets me answer my red line by keeping the Ducted defensive and never calling it the next generation. He also warns that his demonstration dates slipped, so a one-year margin to 2037 is thin. A slip still earns from the ready year, so I accept the risk and keep 2036 a gate, not a promise. Supply: the package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5, and he would keep the Ducted alone if the base can carry only one project. That is my fallback too.

priorities: Safety and readiness come first. We accept no date without test evidence and no launch with an unresolved safety or durability flag. State the Safran gate for every CFM item, with the reason the partner would agree. A defence that keeps an airframer on CFM, or serving every airframer, fits joint practice. A Ducted with no defensive trigger does not [CX-0184, CG-0065, CG-0066, CX-0587].

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Whatever airframe launches this round enters service in 2037 (NGSA, or fps on a 7-year ramp) or 2040 (fps on a 10-year ramp or via Embraer), and its engines pay us in shop visits well into the 2050s. "We don't have a birthright on that next order." [CX-0564] We win by being on every new airframe that launches, with an engine ready before that airframe enters service. We do it without pressing any airframer into an Open Fan wait [CX-0205], without calling a ducted engine our next generation, and without risking the balance sheet or the payout. One call decides this round. Do we believe nobody moves (S1)? Or do we plan for an airframer launch where we may not be selected (S2-S6)? Everything else follows from the grid, and we get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) Confirmed data put the S1 weight above about 0.60, for example a reason on the record why neither airframer launches this round. The package breaks even against GEnx alone at an S1 weight of 0.623 (0.602 with the rest even), and the Ducted against hold at 0.687 (0.662). Dates and readiness are his call. (5) A rival engine launch or selection appears on the public record: volumes-first then passes on the record itself, without the carve-out. (6) Any price or concession language in the statement, or CFM price talk without Safran: terms veto.
cfo.memo:
Larry, I've run every option column by column; your arithmetic holds. The Ducted is +10.17 against hold in S2, +5.58 on your weights and +5.86 equal, negative only above an S1 weight of about 0.69. The package is +10.61 against GEnx alone in S2, +5.94 and +6.55 weighted, with breakeven at about 0.62. Embraer adds 0.00 to +4.88 and never loses inside the package. GEnx is +0.78 as the third project but -1.22 as the second beside a Ducted alone, so if Embraer drops, GEnx drops with it.

On volumes, nobody has agreed a number with us, and the record still reads S1. I pass the Ducted only under hard rule 3 as mapped, judged in S3: +10.17 alone, +13.05 in the package. Embraer gets no carve-out; its S1 gap is $0.00, so please declare it at zero. The premium is $0 in S2 and $0 on either set of weights. If we called S1 expected, it would be $6.00B, above the cap, and I would veto.

Capex is about $1.0B a year against roughly $2.5B of room after the payout, with no rating effect. We are being extremely careful about avoiding overcapitalization, and this fits.

What the case leaves out: S6 at -105.61, $85B below S2. Codes can change before entry, and supplier dates have slipped on us before. But the good news is that each item's downside is capped at its bill.

Book about -$50B, not -$38.70B, and not S2. I concur with the lean.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (date veto ground 1): ready year of every order
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted: launch + 6. Open Fan: launch + 10 and not before 2045. Partner Embraer: counts 7 years after launch. GEnx: counts 3 years after launch and not before 2035. An order whose value depends on an earlier date fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036 (2030+6). The Ducted grid row (-4.00 / -21.90 / -75.51 / -52.61 / -51.70 / -105.50, S1-S6) is priced at 2036 and no earlier. Partner Embraer: launched 2030, counts from 2037 (2030+7), the year after the Ducted is ready. GEnx upgrade: launched 2030. By the rule it would count from 2033, but not before the first re-engine enters service, or 2042. No re-engine is on the record, so the grid counts it from 2042, and never before 2035. Open Fan: held. Launched in 2030 or in 2035 it would be ready in 2045 (the later of launch + 10 and 2045). No order in Culp's lean (option 4: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61) depends on an earlier date.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (date veto ground 2): dates in the frame, statement and other moves
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Ducted ready date before 2036 (launch + 6), no Open Fan entry before 2045, and no RISE fly-demo or flight-test date.
tests.numbers: Dates in Culp's frame: Ducted ready 2036 (2030+6). New-NB entry 2037 (NGSA, or fps on a 7-year ramp) and 2040 (fps on a 10-year ramp, or via Embraer). Open Fan not before 2045. All sit at the board's development times. The statement is not yet written; I recheck every date in it at step 4. Ask (1): on the board, 2036 is the floor, and nothing earlier is acceptable. My record holds no ducted test programme. What is in real testing is the technology base: RISE has completed over 350 tests with an early durability focus [CX-0216]; RISE compact-core HPT blades are in dust testing [CX-0222]; open-fan noise has been tested with Airbus [CX-0013]; and the LEAP-1A HPT fix was turned on and turned off in test, then certified in December 2024 [CX-0009, CX-0225]. So 2036 is a test-gated floor, reported against every round, not a promise (inference).

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Earlier is better, but a late date does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted launched 2030, ready 2036. First new-NB entry 2037 for an NGSA (S2, S3, and the NGSA in S5 and S6) or a 7-year fps: the Ducted is 1 year ahead. Entry 2040 for a 10-year fps (S4) or fps via Embraer: the Ducted is 4 years ahead. The +10 pp counts from 2037 (S2, S3, S5, S6) or 2040 (S4). A 2035 launch would be ready only in 2041: 4 years after a 2037 entry and 1 year after a 2040 entry. Track record: my demonstration-type dates slipped (the RISE fly demo moved from mid-decade to 'this decade'; the LEAP-1B kit ran about a year late), so a 1-year margin is thin. A 1-year slip still meets 2037, and a longer slip still earns from its ready year.

tests.threshold: An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry avoids the board's loss. Ready after it, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with lobbying). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Launched in 2030 or in 2035, it is ready in 2045 either way (launch + 10, and not before 2045). First new-NB entry this round: 2037 (8 years before 2045) or 2040 (5 years before). It cannot be ready for either. Open Fan against hold: -8.00 / -57.60 / -35.40 / -41.46 / -51.84 / -16.07 (S1-S6). Open Fan + Lobby + GEnx against GEnx alone: -11.00 / -39.34 / -35.05 / -35.87 / -40.75 / -18.01. Culp's lean holds the Open Fan, so his plan does not fail this test. Ask (2), RISE status: real testing is under way [CX-0013, CX-0216, CX-0222]. The evidence shows no open durability failure, but it ends in October 2025. The ground and flight test is set for 'this decade' and is not yet reported [CX-0211].

tests.name: Physics: the 20% line and the Ducted's wording
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A Ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so it is never called the next generation; that it is defensive only, under hard rule 3, is company doctrine. The brief has no fuel-burn data, so this is a wording check unless a fuel-burn claim is made (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief makes no fuel-burn claim. Culp's frame calls the Ducted a defence under H3 (trigger: S3 and S6 on the grid), never the next generation, and keeps RISE whole. Ask (4), confirmed: 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan', and a ducted engine has 'less than half the fuel burn improvements' of an open fan, which is rated at 'more than 20%' [CX-0001]. So the Ducted will not meet 20%. The 20% red line binds RISE as the next generation. For the Ducted it is answered by the defensive framing, not struck. I recheck the statement's wording at step 4.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. The brief has no durability data, so this is not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: The brief has no durability data, and Culp's frame makes no durability claim. Ask (3): I raise no safety or durability flag. The Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade durability against. The trade to watch is schedule, given the 1-year margin to a 2037 entry. The rule I hold: durability holds the date, not the reverse. If testing shows 2036 needs a durability shortcut, the date moves and I report it as a flag. The LEAP lesson: 9,882 cycles against about 17,000 for the CFM56 in benign conditions, and about 4,800 against 7,000-8,000 in harsh ones, fixed only at shop visits over years [CX-0006, CX-0649]. Confirmed: no durability traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].

GEnx as the third project, against Ducted + Partner Embraer: +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. Ask (5): 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. Raw materials are not on the board; they are a judgement for my seat. Sequencing staggers the physical load: Ducted development 2030-36, Embraer volume from 2037, GEnx counting from 2042 with no re-engine on the record. I have no test showing it removes the board's strain. If the base can carry one project: the Ducted alone. If two: Ducted + Partner Embraer, which beats Ducted + GEnx in S2-S6.

vetoes.plan: Public statement and other moves (not yet written; I check them at step 4)
vetoes.ground: No veto now. At step 4, on my date ground (binding ground 2), I would veto any statement or other move that gives a Ducted ready date before 2036, an Open Fan entry before 2045, or any RISE fly-demo, ground-test or flight-test date. Such a date rests on analysis, not test. My veto right over programme dates is an inference from my 2024 standard for believing durability-fix results [CX-0009, CX-0008]. The team rule makes a failed date test bind unless Culp answers it with evidence. Separately, as advice on physics: never call the Ducted our next generation [CX-0183].

ops.would_change_mind_if: Only test or field data changes my mind, never analysis or a forecast. (a) Ducted turn-on, turn-off milestones (core and hot-section durability tests) show 2036 cannot be met without trading durability: I hold the durability, not the date, report the slip, and the Board reads it as a flag that the cross-functional team must close before the launch stands. (b) A durability failure is reproduced in RISE compact-core or hot-section testing: the flag goes to the cross-functional team, and no launch builds on that hardware until it is turned off in test. (c) Supplier field data on the 9 constrained suppliers show they cannot carry Ducted development on top of the LEAP ramp: the Ducted goes alone, and Partner Embraer and GEnx are held. (d) An airframer on the record commits to an entry no earlier than 2045: then the Open Fan's readiness test passes and I would test a launch by 2035. ops.memo:
Real testing, not analysis. Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036, launch plus six. That is the board's development time and a floor; nothing earlier. It clears a 2037 NGSA or 7-year fps by one year, a 2040 fps by four. I have no ducted test programme to show you. What is in real testing is the base: RISE, over 350 tests with an early durability focus, compact-core HPT blades in dust testing, and the LEAP hot-section fix we turned on and turned off. So 2036 is a gate, not a promise, reported against every round. My record: test-backed fixes on time, demonstration dates late. One year of slip still meets 2037.

No safety or durability flag. The Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade durability against; durability holds the date, never the reverse. No single person can make a safety decision: gate calls are cross-functional.

Physics: 20% is practically impossible without the open fan, and a ducted engine gets less than half the gain. The Ducted is a defence under hard rule 3, not our next generation. Larry's 20% line stands for RISE.

Open Fan: ready 2045 at the earliest, launched 2030 or 2035; eight years after a 2037 entry. Hold. I promise no demo date; mine slipped.

Supply, Embraer and the expected column: no evidence, following doctrine and Culp. The package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65 over the Ducted alone); Ducted plus GEnx does not (-1.22). If the base carries one project, keep the Ducted.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: nobody has launched a new narrowbody yet. When one comes, we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM, together with our partners at Safran, is launching a new ducted engine now. That way a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first. We don't expect it ready before 2036. We'll report against that gate every year, on test, not on slides. It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE. We're all in on that technology, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

CFM is also teaming with Embraer. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, GE is upgrading the GEnx for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: when the airframers move, and what they pick. So we plan on the low case, and we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Do Nothing costs $32.07B (S2) to $105.01B (S6) in every column where an airframer launches. A new NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040. We have no birthright on that order [CX-0564]. We win by having a new CFM engine ready before that entry, offered to every airframer. We don't press anyone into an Open Fan wait, and we keep the payout whole.

HARD RULE 3 TRIGGER (named): S3, where an NGSA on code 2 takes Airbus's whole slot from CFM; also S6 (codes 1 and 2). It is on the grid, not yet on the public record. Ghai passes the Ducted's volumes-first test under this carve-out (+10.17 alone, +13.05 in the package in S3).

- The weighted value is positive unless S1 carries more than about 62%.
- Timing is now or never for this round's airframes: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036, one year ahead of a 2037 entry, while a 2035 launch is ready only in 2041. A late Ducted still earns from its ready year, but S3 is the slot where being late costs most.

Durability is not traded [CX-0208]: Ali raises no safety or durability flag; the Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade against; and durability holds the date, never the reverse. Gate reviews are cross-functional [CX-0012].

- Ducted: consent assumed. A defence that keeps an airframer on CFM fits joint practice in serving both airframers [CX-0185, CX-0587]. Safran shares 50-50 in the installed-base annuity at risk in S3. There is no price talk, and RISE, the joint next generation, is untouched.

- Open Fan and Lobby: held, so nothing to gate.
- GEnx: GE alone, no gate.

MONEY (Ghai):

- Against about $2.55B of room after a 70%+ return of about $8.5B free cash flow [CX-0645], headroom is $1.55B. No debt, no rating effect.
- Premium is $0.00 in S2 and on both sets of weights.

SUPPLY (Ali): the package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65 over the Ducted alone). If the base can carry only one project, the Ducted goes alone.

STANDING COMMITMENT FOR THE BOARD REVIEW: if Partner Embraer is vetoed, GEnx goes with it (-1.22 as the second project), leaving the Ducted alone. If the Ducted is vetoed, Embraer falls and I run GEnx upgrade alone (+0.78).

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove Embraer, Lobby, GEnx as the third project, and the cancel path. My record never addresses Embraer or lobbying (profile §6; dashboard_game §2, §5).

NEXT ROUND: I will look at the airframer launches and selections on the record. If no threat appears by 2035, a cancel writes off $3.33B to save $0.67B, so the decision is judged then on its own grid, never for RISE.

ORDERS
- Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036 (launch + 6). That is 1 year before the earliest new-NB entry (2037: an NGSA, or an fps on a 7-year ramp). It is 4 years before 2040 (an fps on a 10-year ramp, or via Embraer).
- Partner Embraer: counts from 2037 (2030 + 7). The Ducted it needs is ready in 2036.
- GEnx upgrade: 2033 by rule, but the grid counts it from 2042 because no re-engine is on the record. It never counts before 2035, since a re-engine launched in 2030 enters service in 2035.
- Open Fan: held. Launched in 2030 or in 2035, it would be ready in 2045 either way.
- Lobby: held.
No order's value rests on an earlier year, so Test 1 passes.

STATEMENT AND OTHER MOVES
- The only date in the statement is 'not ready before 2036', reported each year 'on test, not on slides'. That is a floor, not a promise.
- There is no Open Fan entry date ('really not for us to say'). There is no RISE fly-demo, ground-test or flight-test date.
- The private gate-review move carries 2036 as a test-gated floor.
Test 2 passes. The physics wording also passes: 'It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE.'

FLAGS FOR THE BOARD (not vetoes)
1. Safety and durability: I raise no flag. The cross-functional gate reviews, with Safran's engineers, answer my safety-call test: no single person makes a safety decision [CX-0012]. Durability holds the date, never the reverse [CX-0208].
2. Readiness margin (advice): the line 'a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first' holds on the numbers, 2036 against 2037, but the margin is 1 year. My test-backed fixes landed on time; my demonstration dates did not. The fly demo moved from mid-decade to 'this decade', and the LEAP-1B kit ran about a year late [CX-0151, CX-0211, CX-0210]. If 2036 slips, we report it in the next round, and a late Ducted still earns +10 pp from its ready year.
3. Supply load (No evidence: following doctrine): the package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5 but not in S1 or S6. If the 9 suppliers behind 80% of shortages [CX-0613] cannot carry it, the Ducted goes alone, as Culp's standing commitment provides.

We find problems before problems find us.

recommendations.text: Safety and readiness come first. Report the 2036 Ducted date to us every round as a test-gated floor, with core and hot-section results that were turned on and turned off in test, and with gate calls made cross-functionally alongside Safran's engineers. The margin to a 2037 entry is one year, and Ali's own demonstration dates have slipped. If testing shows that 2036 needs a durability shortcut, the date moves, and it comes to us as a flag before the next round's orders, never as a traded durability margin.

Quality and supply. Complete the readiness work on the 9 suppliers and 15 sites before the ducted development load lands, so that LEAP deliveries and spares are not crowded out. If the base can carry only one project, bring us the Ducted alone, and drop Partner Embraer and GEnx together: GEnx as the second project beside a Ducted alone loses $1.22B.

Keep RISE whole as technology. The RISE allowance is unused. On the public rules, any narrowbody launched in the 2035 round enters service by 2042-2045, so a 2035 Open Fan has an airframer path only if the grid shows no wait penalty in any plausible column. Bring it to us only on that showing. Otherwise say plainly that the 'Introduce the Open Fan' objective is given up on the dashboard. We will not stretch the airframer-path test, and RISE is never cancelled for cost.

Next round, re-test the Ducted on the record. If an airframer has launched and selected, show the item against its default on the new grid. If none has, any cancel must pass our cancellation test: at least zero in every plausible column. Remember that a 2035 cancel writes off $3.33B to save $0.67B. Re-set the column weights from the bulletin: the package breaks even at an S1 weight of about 0.62. Show any Joint Venture commitment (CFM -10 pp) or rival engine launch, which this round's columns leave out.

Keep the payout whole. This round commits $1.0B a year of the roughly $2.5B of room left after returning at least 70% of about $8.5B in 2028 free cash flow, which leaves about $1.5B a year for later rounds. The premium is $0 of the $4.0B game cap. Keep booking expected PV low (-50.41), and do not raise it until a selection is on the record.

The Safran gate. Confirm the Ducted and the Embraer teaming through CFM's joint practice, and present both in public as CFM decisions taken with Safran. The statement does this for the Ducted, but it says only 'CFM is also teaming with Embraer'. Any Embraer price or terms are a joint decision.

The public statement passes our disclosure test: it names no rival, blames no one, gives no Open Fan date and has no price talk. In later statements, keep 2036 as a floor rather than a promise, and never call the Ducted the next generation.

board_review.note: The Board approves all three items, having checked them against the brief's grid. The package is the best plan in S2-S5 and on both weight sets, so the premium is $0. The Ducted is +10.61 in the expected column, S2, and loses at most its $6B bill (S1). Partner Embraer is 0.00 to +4.88, never negative. The GEnx upgrade is +0.77 to +0.78 in every column as the third project. Ali confirms 2036 as launch plus six and raises no safety or durability flag. The rationale rebuts the 20% line by keeping the Ducted defensive, with RISE whole. Ghai's one failed test, volumes first on Embraer, is answered at $0.00, and he concurs. The commitments total $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room. Safran's consent is assumed by joint practice for the Ducted (a hard-rule-3 defence) and for Embraer (which serves every airframer). We will watch the one-year margin to 2037 and the supply load.
