Severe-environment testing starts early, all life-limited parts are at full life at EIS, and the six-year programme is not compressed. Eddy's ground-1 veto stands on any order or statement that dates GTF2 before 2036. Fleet recovery keeps first call on powder metal, castings and MRO slots [PX-0080].

other_moves.move: Standing 2035 review
other_moves.detail: We write three tests into the plan. (1) Re-test gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected against any airframe launched in 2030 or 2035; a 2035 trigger is ready in 2041, in time for any EIS of 2042 or later. (2) Test the Joint Venture trigger: Rolls-Royce's commitment on the public record, or a live airframe with code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A commit must share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233], and a live GTF2's spend folds in. (3) Run a cancel test on any live GTF2 if an airframer drops P&W's code before EIS. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch stays in reserve.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: Pratt & Whitney has no new engine programme to announce today, and our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% for four years. That is not where we want to be. We know we have to earn the dependable-engine reputation every day, so the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. Control what you can control. Our commitment is this. In any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside another engine, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and full-life parts proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We will not buy a selection: standard terms, no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we ever enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core technology. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold, premium_b 0. One Board item: launch_if_selected.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. I start from Eddy's proposal: launch_if_selected / hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders.

2. I strike every plan that fails a binding veto.
- C (launch / hold) and E (launch / commit) fail Mitchill's ground 2, carrying an unselected engine. On his weights the edge over launch_if_selected is 3.79 x 0.18 - 2.00 x 0.45 = -0.22. With the 2035 cancel ($1.67B write-off) written in, it is -0.07. Both are below my bar of 0 and the Board's +0.50. The veto binds, and no premium can buy a hedge that fails it.
- D and E (any jv_with_rr commit) fail his ground 4, booking upside before it is proven. The commit's whole case rests on a Rolls-Royce commitment and a code-4 selection, and neither is on the record.
- Eddy invokes no veto. Durability and parts pass for A to E.
- Plans left: A (hold / hold) and B (launch_if_selected / hold).

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035].
- A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA and fps 7-year enter service in 2037 (a 1-year margin); fps 10-year and Embraer in 2040 (4 years). B passes by construction, because it triggers only where GTF2 is ready by EIS.
- I take Eddy's warning on the 1-year NGSA margin seriously. It equals his own Advantage slip, and my operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024]. That is my optimism bias, so I discount it. The constraint I set:
  - GTF2 is an Advantage derivative;
  - the programme is not compressed;
  - every life-limited part is at full life at EIS;
  - we give no public date before 2036;
  - if test data later show the EIS cannot be met, Eddy's ground-1 veto binds.

4. Optimise on Mitchill's weights.
- Expected PV: B +3.15; C +2.94 (vetoed); D +2.91 (vetoed); A -14.02.
- B weakly dominates hold in every column. Its value against hold:
  - S1 0
  - S2 +50.49
  - S3 0
  - S4 +22.16
  - S5 +49.76
  - S6 0
  - S7 0
- Weighted value against hold: +17.18.

MY TESTS
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: pass. The commitment coincides with a selection; nothing is spent on an unnamed engine.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: the loss is large. NGSA without P&W costs -27.76 under every order. B lets us answer any selection this round (codes 2, 6, 7), which is what the test requires. The hedge would claw back only 3.79 of the 27.76 in S3 and S6; most of those columns are Airbus's choice, won with product and time on wing, not by spending early. Applying "miss a cycle" to GTF2 is inference: I said it of RTX's businesses generally.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine-favoured order is also the best expected-PV order. Premium 0.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081][P-0669]: pass. If triggered, about $0.33B a year is 5.5% of a roughly $6B envelope. No stretch is needed, and the debt path is intact (Mitchill).
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: pass. Standard terms, and the kit is sold.
- Tie-breaks:
  - The fleet beats a new engine: B takes no engineers or parts until a selection.
  - A rival's discount: none is on the record, and none would move this answer.

RED-LINE FLAGS AND HOW I TREATED THEM
- Sole source [P-0746]: every trigger code on the grid is shared (S2 code 6; S4 code 7; S5 codes 7 and 6). I accept shared-source selections on NGSA and fps as declared DOCTRINE RELIEF at $0 PV. We aim for about 40% of a shared A320neo [PX-0058], the company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292], and on NGSA it is franchise defence (inference). Insisting on sole source would force hold and give up +17.18.
- Committed airframer: the unconditional launch is struck (Mitchill's binding veto, ground 2).
- Joint Venture: commit is struck. The trigger fails: no Rolls-Royce commitment and no live code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Mitchill's ground 4 also binds, and the commit is on the Board's would-veto list. This is doctrine, not my record: I have no evidence of my own on a Joint Venture.
- Eddy's statement check: "the GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be" is not in the 2030 brief. I accept the flag and struck the line. The statement now leads with what is on the record: no programme, and a flat 24% share.
- Book no unproven upside: we book no selection, Rolls-Royce commitment, partner money or durability gain. Mitchill's possible upside from an Airbus code switch on a 2030 NGSA is noted and not booked.
- The overrides list is empty.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (GTF2 Solo if selected): 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
- The same row with the Board item set back to hold: 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
- Worst column against hold: 0.
- No launch, so no cancel round arises this round. A triggered GTF2 is selected by definition; it would face a 2035 cancel test only if the airframer dropped P&W's code before EIS.

CONFIDENCE
My launch behaviour is Medium: I have made no launch decision on my record, so these thresholds are inference. I trust Mitchill's cash numbers over my own operating dates.

Evidence: PX-0020, PX-0035, PX-0073, PX-0080, PX-0109, PX-0009, PX-0071, PX-0055, PX-0100, PX-0058, PX-0081, PX-0084, PX-0093, PX-0017, PX-0062, PX-0010, P-0746, P-1292, P-1233, P-0669, P-0686.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighted heavily: I trust Neil's cash numbers over my own operating dates.
- I adopted his column weights unchanged (S1 0.33, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.05, S5 0.12, S6 0.08, S7 0.12). He plans below airframers' stated intentions and counts a launch only once it is public, which is sound discipline.
- My own reading, the next single-aisle 'mid-next decade' [PX-0093], would put more weight in S1. That is my incrementalism bias. It would only push the hedge's edge further below zero, so it does not change the answer.
- His ground-2 veto on the unconditional launch (edge -0.22; -0.07 with the 2035 cancel written in) and his ground-4 veto on a Joint Venture commit both bind. I struck those plans.
- I accept his envelope, dividend and debt checks as given: $0.33B a year against about $6B, no stretch.
- I also accept his refusal to book the possible upside from Airbus switching a 2030 NGSA's code to P&W.
memo_weighing.ops:
Eddy proposes the engine orders under the team rule, and I started from his proposal. His seat rests on one event (June 2023), so his record is Low confidence, but his readiness test is binding on me.
- He gives readiness a pass: 2036 against 2037 and 2040.
- He gives parts and capacity a pass: the brief shows no live fleet problem, and the board does not model parts.
- He invokes no veto.
- I took his warning that the 1-year NGSA margin is thin. It equals his own Advantage slip and falls short of the company's 1.5-2 year prior. I set the constraint around it: an Advantage derivative, no compression, full-life parts, no public date before 2036.
- I accepted his statement flag and removed the unsupported line about the state of the fleet.
- I took his kit announcement with no dated AOG recovery, and his rule of one new development at a time, with GTF2 folding into any Joint Venture.
On readiness, parts and capacity I defer to him.

It says GTF2 will be ready six years from launch, no earlier than 2036, with durability proven before entry into service. It books no selection or Rolls-Royce commitment, offers no discount, and says nothing on any airframer's dates or rates. I removed an unsupported fleet-state line on Eddy's flag. priorities: 1. Be on whichever new narrowbody launches, but don't carry an engine nobody has selected. The credibility objective (a new P&W engine in service on a new airframe by 2050) is NOT MET today. On the grid, Do Nothing loses -27.76 if NGSA launches without P&W (S2, S3, S5, S6) and -2.85 if fps launches (S4). The Board's preferred form is gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected (sole source on a committed airframe, invest 'when we've seen it') [P-0746, P-0737, P-1347, P-1367].

2. A return above the hurdle against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Each Board item's weighted value against hold must be >= 0 on the grid. The grid discounts at 10%, which is above the 8% of the 2017 intrinsic-value model. No premium should be needed this round [P-0731, P-0715, P-1165, PG-0024].

3. Durability and readiness before entry into service, and the GTF fleet before a new engine. GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. Every possible EIS is later: NGSA or fps 7-year in 2037, fps 10-year or via Embraer in 2040. Time on wing must come ahead of fuel burn [P-1360, P-1214, PG-0050].

4. Keep the dividend whole and debt on its pre-ASR path. GTF2 costs about $0.33B a year, 5-6% of the roughly $6B self-funded envelope. No envelope stretch is needed this round, and the Board keeps its once-in-the-game stretch in reserve [P-0566, P-0686, P-0499, PX-0268].
5. Commit to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce only on a public trigger, and then share risk, never the gear or core technology [P-1233, P-1875, PG-0047].

- Mitchill's weights show 3.79 x P(S3+S6) - 2.00 x P(S1+S7) >= +0.50. That needs P(S3+S6) >= 0.43 if the rest of the weight sits in S1 and S7; break-even is 0.35.

Its worst column against hold is -2.00 (S1, S7), which equals its own bill, so Bounded downside passes. Launch is identical to launch_if_selected in S2, S4 and S5, so its case can rest only on S3 and S6 (+3.79).

recommendations.text: Miss a cycle: order gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected this round. It is never worse than Do Nothing, and it gains +50.49 (S2), +22.16 (S4) and +49.76 (S5) if an airframer names P&W. It costs nothing otherwise and serves the 2050 credibility objective. It also keeps 'Capitalise on the GTF' (ΔPV >= 0) met in S1 and S7, where an unconditional launch would sit at -2.00.

If the ExCo weighs an unconditional launch to defend the A320neo franchise against an NGSA without P&W, show the Board the edge column by column against launch_if_selected. Only S3 and S6 (+3.79) and S1 and S7 (-2.00) differ. Show that the edge is at least +$0.50B, write the 2035 cancel test into the plan ($1.67B write-off if no airframe has named P&W), and record Mitchill's position on carrying an unselected engine.

Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Set premium_b to 0 unless a gap is declared with its reason; any gap must be at most $0.5B, must serve the objective and must stay inside the company's $1B cap. Money that does not clear the 10% grid is better spent buying back stock.

Hold the Joint Venture this round as a standing option. Bring it back in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframer lists code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Any Joint Venture must share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology. Rolls-Royce's own executives said a Joint Venture holds only while both partners are on the same new engine. With GTF2 live, a later commit should fold in GTF2's spend rather than add new R&D.

Durability before entry into service. Eddy's memo should show the GTF2 durability and time-on-wing programme and its 2036 ready year against each live EIS. It should also confirm that GTF fleet parts and recovery come first, so that the 2016-2023 entry-into-service problems are not repeated.

Keep the dividend and debt path whole. GTF2's roughly $0.33B a year fits the self-funded envelope of about $6B, so no stretch is needed; keep the one-round stretch for later in the game. Mitchill should confirm the dividend is covered and debt is on its pre-ASR path.

Disclosure. The public statement should offer GTF2 to any airframer that names P&W, ready six years after launch, which means no EIS before 2036. It should claim no durability not yet proven, say nothing on airframers' dates, and book no selection or Rolls-Royce commitment. If a shared code (6 or 7) can trigger GTF2, the CEO should declare the shared-source choice as doctrine relief in his rationale.

frame.question: Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Nothing has launched and no selection is on the record. Airbus and Boeing will choose their engines in their own rounds; that part is not ours to control. What is ours: whether we can answer a selection the moment it comes, with a GTF2 that is durable and ready by the airframe's EIS, without carrying an engine nobody has selected and without touching the dividend. So the question for 2030 is this. Which gtf2_solo order (hold, launch_if_selected or launch) and which jv_with_rr order (hold or commit) lets us take any NGSA or fps selection that names P&W this round? Each must pass the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035], then Neil's payback and return gate, then the Board. Second question: is there a franchise-defence case for an unconditional launch against an NGSA that goes ahead without us? On this grid that is the only column set where launch beats launch_if_selected.
frame.situation:
Public record, 2030: no programme launched; everyone is on today's products. The 737 MAX flies LEAP-1B and the A320neo flies GTF and LEAP. Observed NB engine share 2026-29 is CFM 76% / P&W 24% / RR 0%, with no change. No engine selections. No Rolls-Royce Joint Venture commitment on the record, and no live airframe with a Rolls-Royce code (1, 4, 5, 7).

Our position (brief): ΔPV +0.00 if nobody moves (EV $110B, WACC 10%, 960 NB engines a year). Objective: Restore credibility is NOT MET (no new P&W engine on a new airframe). Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV >= 0) is MET at +0.00.

Timing (rules): a GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. EIS for an airframe launched this round: NGSA or fps 7-year in 2037, fps 10-year or via Embraer in 2040. GTF2 clears every possible EIS this round; the tightest margin is one year, on NGSA and fps 7-year. A Joint Venture would form only if Rolls-Royce also commits, and would be ready 6 years after formation (2036 at the earliest).

What the grid says (ΔPV $B, S1-S7):
- hold: 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0
- launch_if_selected: 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0. Never below hold; +50.49 (S2), +22.16 (S4), +49.76 (S5).
- launch: -2.00 / +22.73 / -23.97 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -23.97 / -2.00
- Any row + jv commit: identical except S7, where it costs -2.00 unless an unconditional GTF2 is live and folds in.

The miss-a-cycle loss is large [PX-0071][P-1347]. An NGSA without P&W costs -27.76 under any order, and an unconditional launch claws back only +3.79 of that. Most of that column is decided by Airbus's selection, which we win with product and time on wing, not price [PX-0055]. Trigger codes for launch_if_selected this round are shared-source in the grid (S2 code 6, S4 code 7, S5 codes 7 and 6), so the sole-source doctrine [P-0746] needs a declared relief.
levers_in_play: gtf2_solo: hold | launch_if_selected | launch (brief section 3). A 2030 launch is ready in 2036; it can be cancelled in the 2035 round with a write-off of $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B (rules: bill x years elapsed / development years).

jv_with_rr: hold | commit (brief section 3). A commit is public at once and standing. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce also commits, and P&W pays $2B. A live GTF2 folds in and its spend counts toward that $2B. The commit can be withdrawn before formation.
No widebody, pricing-terms or durability-kit order exists on this board. The Hot Section / durability kit can only be an other move with no board effect [PX-0088][PX-0106].
Public statement and other_moves: the conditional, dated offer. I propose the disclosure (team rule).
options_to_test: A. Default: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold. Row 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0. The Board's comparator. It fails my miss-a-cycle test: it cannot answer a selection this round, and it gives up +50.49 in S2, +22.16 in S4 and +49.76 in S5.

frame.asks_cfo:
Neil, I trust your cash numbers over my operating dates. Please bring:
(1) Your own S1-S7 probabilities, summing to 1, with your reasoning on how likely Airbus is to launch NGSA this round and on which code.
(2) For each row A-E: the worst column, the expected PV, and the weighted value against hold. That is the Board's test for every Board item.
(3) launch minus launch_if_selected by column (S1 -2.00, S3 +3.79, S6 +3.79, S7 -2.00, 0 elsewhere) and its expected edge, 3.79 x P(S3+S6) - 2.00 x P(S1+S7), against my bar of >= 0 and the Board's +$0.50B. Mark ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine) passed or failed for an unconditional launch.
(4) The cancel round: a 2030 launch can be cancelled in 2035 at $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B. Confirm that a 2035 launch_if_selected would still serve any NGSA or fps launched in 2035 (ready 2041, EIS 2042 or later). If so, the hedge earns nothing from waiting beyond S3 and S6 this round.
(5) The Joint Venture's cost if Rolls-Royce commits and nobody selects it: -2.00 standalone (S7), and 0 incremental beside a live unconditional GTF2 because it folds in. Confirm.
(6) Whether a triggered launch_if_selected on a shared code (S2, S5) books any upside before it is proven. My reading is that it does not: the selection is the condition.
(7) Envelope and capital order: about $0.33B a year against roughly $6B self-funded [PX-0268], the dividend covered [PX-0081], debt on its pre-ASR path [PX-0353], no stretch, and the return against a buyback at the 10% grid.
(8) Your four veto grounds, each marked passed or failed, for each candidate order.
frame.asks_ops:
Shane, you propose the engine orders.
(1) Your proposal for gtf2_solo and jv_with_rr, with the reasoning.
(2) Readiness: GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036, against NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, and fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040. The NGSA margin is one year. Tell me plainly whether the durability programme (time on wing, LLP life, about 3x the testing, as on the Advantage [PX-0084]) fits inside six years. My own dates have slipped before [PX-0017], so I want your view, not mine.
(3) Joint Venture readiness if it ever forms: 6 years after formation, or earlier with a folded GTF2. Can the gear and core stay ours inside it?
(4) Pacing parts and capacity: powder metal, castings, MRO slots. Confirm that GTF fleet recovery and the AOG curve keep first call, so GTF2 repeats none of the 2016-2023 entry-into-service problems.
(5) The engineering load of GTF2 alongside the Advantage and the durability kit.
(6) Your two veto checks (durability before EIS; parts and capacity), marked passed or failed, for each candidate order.
(7) Whether you want the durability kit announced as a public other move: charged for, not given [PX-0100], with no board effect.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is Option B: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold, premium_b 0.

Why. On the grid, launch_if_selected is never below hold, and it answers any selection that names us this round, codes 2, 6 or 7 (S2, S4, S5 are worth +50.49, +22.16 and +49.76 against hold). It spends nothing otherwise, so Capitalise stays met in S1 and S7, and it is the only route this round to Restore credibility by 2050. It passes my tests:
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: the commitment coincides with the selection.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: we can answer this round.
- Durability: ready in 2036, ahead of every possible EIS, subject to Shane's check.
- Dividend safe: about $0.33B a year if triggered.

The shared-source triggers (codes 6 and 7) are declared as doctrine relief, not a PV premium. A shared NGSA is franchise defence; we already run at about 40% of a shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292].

The unconditional launch (C) is the one open question. It gains only in S3 and S6 (+3.79) and loses $2.00B in S1 and S7. It needs P(S3+S6) of about 0.35 to break even and about 0.43 for the Board. My own record says the next single-aisle comes "mid-next decade" [PX-0093]. That is my incrementalism bias, so I will not lean on it alone: the board gives Airbus a strong reason to move early, and I will take Neil's weights. Even so, P(S3+S6) would require Airbus to launch NGSA this round and to leave us off it. I do not expect that to clear 0.43. I will take C only if Neil's edge clears zero and the Board's +$0.50B, with the 2035 cancel written in.

Joint Venture: hold. No Rolls-Royce commitment on the record and no live code 1/4/5/7. It is a standing option for 2035 on a public trigger, gear and core protected [P-1233]. My lean here is doctrine and inference; I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture.

Proposed disclosure (public_statement): "The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be, and fleet recovery keeps first call on our parts and our engineers. Control what you can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and durability proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Standard terms; we are not in the launch phase on pricing. We will not speak for any airframer's plans or dates."

Proposed other move (public, no board effect): continue the GTF durability kit for the installed fleet, sold, not given.

tests.threshold: One weight per grid column, summing to 1; used for every expected value below
tests.numbers: S1 0.33, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.05, S5 0.12, S6 0.08, S7 0.12 (sum 1.00). Reasoning: P(Airbus launches NGSA this round) = S2+S3+S5+S6 = 0.50. Nothing is on the record. ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo = launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr = hold. (premium_b is not my field; I expect 0.)

(1) WHY.
- gtf2_solo launch_if_selected. It ties GTF2 to a customer. It launches only if a live airframe that is not yet in service names P&W this round (code 2, 6 or 7) and GTF2 would be ready by that airframe's EIS. Otherwise nothing is spent and engineering stays on the fleet.
  - Grid row 'GTF2 Solo if selected': 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
  - Row 'GTF2: hold': 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
  - So it is never below hold. It is also the only route this round to a new P&W engine on a new airframe by 2050.
- jv_with_rr hold. No Rolls-Royce commitment is on the record and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A commit costs -2.00 in S7 (row 'hold + commit to JV') and has no EIS to serve.
- Unconditional launch (Option C) is not my proposal. My lever rule is to launch only into a code with P&W already on the public record, and none is. An undisclosed hedge is Calio's call and Mitchill's gate. I do not veto it: readiness and parts both pass on the brief.
- Shared codes 6 and 7. The doctrine relief is Calio's call. From the operating seat, a shared ramp is easier on pacing parts than a sole-source ramp, because the powder-metal escape came out of a ramp-driven capacity build [P-1040] (inference).

(2) READINESS.
- A GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. Against NGSA 2037 and fps 7-year 2037, the margin is 1 year: pass. Against fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040, the margin is 4 years: pass.
- Does the durability programme fit inside six years? On the board, yes. In my judgement, it fits only under four conditions:
  - GTF2 is a derivative on the Advantage architecture, with the gear and core already matured and the roughly 3x testing approach reused [PX-0084].
  - Hot, sandy severe-environment testing starts early [PX-0122][PX-0128].
  - All life-limited parts are at full life at EIS.
  - Nothing is compressed.
- The 1-year NGSA margin is about what the Advantage slipped on my own date (mid-2024 planned, certified 2025 [PX-0128][P-0785]). It is short of the company's +1.5-2 year slip prior for a derivative (profile.md section 3).
- Result: pass, but thin on NGSA and comfortable on fps 10-year. We give no public date earlier than 2036, and we do not speak for the airframer's EIS.

(3) JOINT VENTURE READINESS.
- If it forms in 2030 (S7), it is ready in 2036, with or without a folded 2030 GTF2.
- If it forms in 2035, it is ready in 2041. That is still before the EIS of any airframe launched in 2035 (2042 or later), so holding to 2035 costs no readiness.
- Gear and core stay ours only if the Joint Venture shares risk and investment, with module ownership and no technology licence [P-1233]. If a Joint Venture design needs our gear or core handed over, I propose withdraw.
- This is doctrine. I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture.

(4) PACING PARTS AND CAPACITY.
- The brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem: P&W's narrowbody share is flat at 24.0% over 2026-29, at 960 engines a year. The board does not model parts. Result: pass.
- Fleet recovery and the AOG curve keep first call [PX-0080][PX-0123]:
  - Under launch_if_selected, nothing draws on powder metal, castings or MRO slots until a selection.
  - If it triggers, development hardware comes in test-article quantities, and production parts for GTF2 are allocated against the fleet on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0131].
- How we avoid repeating 2016-2023:
  - All development testing done before EIS, and new features instrumented [P-1214][PX-0168].
  - Severe-environment testing, and full-life life-limited parts at EIS [PX-0128].
  - Powder-metal capacity ramped with records discipline [P-1040][PX-0039].
- I have no 2030 AOG count or pacing-parts list, and I will not invent one.

(5) ENGINEERING LOAD. This board charges no strain, so this is my judgement.
- The Advantage was certified in 2025 [P-0785], the kit goes into shop visits from 2026 [PX-0088][PX-0106], and Advantage engineering is shifting to other priorities [PX-0351].
- A 2030 GTF2 does not overlap the kit's first years.
- One new development at a time: GTF2 is the one. If a Joint Venture forms, GTF2 folds into it, so it stays one programme.

(6) MY TWO VETO CHECKS BY OPTION (durability / parts):
- A (hold / hold): pass / pass. Nothing is launched.
- B (launch_if_selected / hold): pass / pass.
- C (launch / hold): pass (ready 2036, EIS 2037) / pass (no live problem in the brief). Not proposed, not vetoed.
- D (launch_if_selected / commit): pass / pass. The Joint Venture serves no live EIS, but that is not one of my grounds.
- E (launch / commit): pass / pass. GTF2 folds in, so it is one programme; also not one of my grounds.
- No binding veto this round.

(7) DURABILITY KIT. Yes, announce it as a public other move: sold, not given [PX-0100], with no board effect. It should carry no dated AOG recovery. The brief gives me no 2030 count, and my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0115][PX-0128].

STATEMENT CHECK.
- 'Ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and durability proven before entry into service' passes my full-life test.
- 'The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be' is not in the 2030 brief. That is Calio's call. If he says it, it is one more reason that launch_if_selected, not launch, is the right form.

My proposal: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold.

Readiness. A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA or fps 7-year enters service in 2037, fps 10-year or via Embraer in 2040. Both pass. On NGSA the margin is one year. That's about what the Advantage slipped on my own date, mid-2024 to 2025, and it's short of the company's 1.5-to-2-year slip prior for a derivative. decision.public_statement: Pratt & Whitney has no new engine programme to announce today, and our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% for four years. That is not where we want to be. We know we have to earn the dependable-engine reputation every day, so the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. Control what you can control. Our commitment is this. In any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside another engine, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and full-life parts proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We will not buy a selection: standard terms, no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we ever enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core technology. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold, premium_b 0. One Board item: launch_if_selected.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. I start from Eddy's proposal: launch_if_selected / hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders.

2. I strike every plan that fails a binding veto.
- C (launch / hold) and E (launch / commit) fail Mitchill's ground 2, carrying an unselected engine. On his weights the edge over launch_if_selected is 3.79 x 0.18 - 2.00 x 0.45 = -0.22. With the 2035 cancel ($1.67B write-off) written in, it is -0.07. Both are below my bar of 0 and the Board's +0.50. The veto binds, and no premium can buy a hedge that fails it.
- D and E (any jv_with_rr commit) fail his ground 4, booking upside before it is proven. The commit's whole case rests on a Rolls-Royce commitment and a code-4 selection, and neither is on the record.
- Eddy invokes no veto. Durability and parts pass for A to E.
- Plans left: A (hold / hold) and B (launch_if_selected / hold).

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035].
- A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA and fps 7-year enter service in 2037 (a 1-year margin); fps 10-year and Embraer in 2040 (4 years). B passes by construction, because it triggers only where GTF2 is ready by EIS.
- I take Eddy's warning on the 1-year NGSA margin seriously. It equals his own Advantage slip, and my operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024]. That is my optimism bias, so I discount it. The constraint I set:
  - GTF2 is an Advantage derivative;
  - the programme is not compressed;
  - every life-limited part is at full life at EIS;
  - we give no public date before 2036;
  - if test data later show the EIS cannot be met, Eddy's ground-1 veto binds.

4. Optimise on Mitchill's weights.
- Expected PV: B +3.15; C +2.94 (vetoed); D +2.91 (vetoed); A -14.02.
- B weakly dominates hold in every column. Its value against hold:
  - S1 0
  - S2 +50.49
  - S3 0
  - S4 +22.16
  - S5 +49.76
  - S6 0
  - S7 0
- Weighted value against hold: +17.18.

MY TESTS
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: pass. The commitment coincides with a selection; nothing is spent on an unnamed engine.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: the loss is large. NGSA without P&W costs -27.76 under every order. B lets us answer any selection this round (codes 2, 6, 7), which is what the test requires. The hedge would claw back only 3.79 of the 27.76 in S3 and S6; most of those columns are Airbus's choice, won with product and time on wing, not by spending early. Applying "miss a cycle" to GTF2 is inference: I said it of RTX's businesses generally.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine-favoured order is also the best expected-PV order. Premium 0.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081][P-0669]: pass. If triggered, about $0.33B a year is 5.5% of a roughly $6B envelope. No stretch is needed, and the debt path is intact (Mitchill).
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: pass. Standard terms, and the kit is sold.
- Tie-breaks:
  - The fleet beats a new engine: B takes no engineers or parts until a selection.
  - A rival's discount: none is on the record, and none would move this answer.

RED-LINE FLAGS AND HOW I TREATED THEM
- Sole source [P-0746]: every trigger code on the grid is shared (S2 code 6; S4 code 7; S5 codes 7 and 6). I accept shared-source selections on NGSA and fps as declared DOCTRINE RELIEF at $0 PV. We aim for about 40% of a shared A320neo [PX-0058], the company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292], and on NGSA it is franchise defence (inference). Insisting on sole source would force hold and give up +17.18.
- Committed airframer: the unconditional launch is struck (Mitchill's binding veto, ground 2).
- Joint Venture: commit is struck. The trigger fails: no Rolls-Royce commitment and no live code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Mitchill's ground 4 also binds, and the commit is on the Board's would-veto list. This is doctrine, not my record: I have no evidence of my own on a Joint Venture.
- Eddy's statement check: "the GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be" is not in the 2030 brief. I accept the flag and struck the line. The statement now leads with what is on the record: no programme, and a flat 24% share.
- Book no unproven upside: we book no selection, Rolls-Royce commitment, partner money or durability gain. Mitchill's possible upside from an Airbus code switch on a 2030 NGSA is noted and not booked.
- The overrides list is empty.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (GTF2 Solo if selected): 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
- The same row with the Board item set back to hold: 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
- Worst column against hold: 0.

Any Joint Venture shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology. A live GTF2's spend folds in and adds no new R&D.

rolls_royce.rationale:
So, the decision, by the team rule.

1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL. ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_pw, ultrafan_wb and t1000_upgrade all at hold. Nothing is on the public record: no fps, no NGSA, no Re-engine, no P&W commitment. Only this round's conditional can catch an airframe launched in 2030, because a 2035 UltraFan is ready in 2042, too late for 2037 or 2040.

2. BINDING VETO CHECKS.
- CFO: McCabe co-signs the conditional against the hurdle. The selected columns are +28.24 to +44.54 on an $8B bill, and the expected gain is +3.37 on the weights she confirmed. She withholds her signature on the unconditional Solo, a Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB and the Trent 1000 upgrade (alone or beside the conditional). None of them is ordered. She invokes no balance-sheet veto: no equity, no borrowing, no buyback leverage.
- Civil: Watson invokes no Civil veto. The zero margin of a 2030 trigger (ready 2037) against a 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps (EIS 2037) is a pass with a note. Against a 10-year fps or fps via Embraer (2040) there are three years in hand. The order triggers only if UltraFan is ready by EIS, so nothing is compressed.
- Support: his concurrence rests on the support plan before EIS, carried here and in other_moves. If triggered: partner MRO shops on the Singapore joint-venture model near launch operators, with no own narrowbody MRO scale; repair technology developed alongside the test programme; a spares pool and field-service team for EIS; partner-shop agreements and castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracted with high-performing suppliers by the 2035 round; an EIS-readiness review before EIS. The test pacing is the full seven years: if a phase slips, the engine slips.
- Statement: the public statement gives no EIS earlier than launch + 7, no 2037 next to any airframe, and no airframer date. No veto stands. overrides is empty.

3. GRID, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1/S2/S3/S4/S5/S6/S7/S8). Weights, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.15 (selection 0.10 in total, our rule for 'nothing on the record').

- ultrafan_wb launch, held ('if selected + UltraFan WB' minus 'if selected'): -4.00 in S1, S3, S6 and S7; -9.00 in S2, S4 and S5; -0.90 in S8; expected -4.04. No Re-engine is on the record, and the gap is above the $1B sub-cap.

frame.question: So, the 2030 question, put in cash and quality of earnings: nothing is on the public record. Do we put any cash at risk for narrowbody, widebody or the Trent 1000 this round? Or do we take only the conditional order, which costs nothing unless an airframer names Rolls-Royce on an airframe UltraFan can serve in time? We are not after market share. I will not spend $8B blind on narrowbody, I will not fund widebody without a Re-engine, and the Trent 1000 upgrade goes ahead only if it pays on this board. The one thing this round alone can do is catch an airframe launched in 2030. A 2035 UltraFan is ready in 2042, which is too late for any 2030 airframe.
frame.situation:
Public record, 2030: no programme has been launched. There is no fps, no NGSA, no 787 Re-engine and no A350 Re-engine, so there are no engine selections or codes. P&W has made no Joint Venture commitment. Markets 2026-29 sit at the status quo: narrowbody Boeing 40 / Airbus 60; narrowbody engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0; widebody engines GE 42 / RR 58.

Our position on hold: ΔPV +0.00, yield 100.0% (EV $110B, debt $40B, WACC 10%).

Objective: narrowbody entry is NOT met (RR narrowbody share 0% in 2045 and 2050). Widebody dominance is MET (58% every year to 2060; worst year 58%).

Timing that decides this round:
- An UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037.
- An NGSA or a 7-year fps launched in 2030 enters service in 2037. That is zero margin.
- A 10-year fps or fps via Embraer enters service in 2040. That is three years of margin.
- A 2035 UltraFan is ready in 2042, too late for any 2030 airframe. A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2041: too late for a 2030 airframe, in time for a 2035 one.
- 2035 is the last round whose narrowbody launch can deliver by 2045.

Grid facts against the hold row (columns S1-S8):
- 'UltraFan NB if selected': 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is never below hold.
- Unconditional 'UltraFan NB Solo': -8.00 in S1, S7 and S8; +3.57 in S3 and S6, because the board credits RR +15 pp once any new narrowbody flies, even if we are not selected; the selected columns match the conditional.
- Trent 1000 upgrade alone: -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8. With no Re-engine it counts only from 2042.
- UltraFan WB alone: -4.00, or -0.90 in S8.
- Joint Venture commit alone: -4.00 in S7 only.
- Beside a triggered UltraFan NB, the $5B strain takes the upgrade to -5.98 against the conditional, and UltraFan WB to -9.00.

Board (risk aversion 4 of 5, time horizon 2.5):
- Would approve `launch_if_selected` with everything else at hold.
- Would approve the upgrade alone only as a declared premium, and does not recommend it.
- Would veto an unconditional Solo, a first Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB, and the upgrade beside any UltraFan order.

RR gains 15 pp of narrowbody once a new narrowbody is in service. `launch_if_selected` triggers only if a live airframe selects a code with RR this round (1, 5, 7) and UltraFan is ready by its EIS; otherwise nothing is spent. No `ultrafan_wb` without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan. Never beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected. Any UltraFan WB premium is capped at $1B [R-1574, R-0929]. The Board would veto it.

`cancel` only a programme no live airframe flies. There is nothing to cancel in 2030 [R-1573].
No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column (NB Solo -$8B, Joint Venture -$4B, UltraFan WB -$4B, upgrade -$2B).

cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then we said the balance sheet. Nothing is on the public record, so no cash goes at risk unless an airframer asks for it.

The conditional order is zero wherever we are not selected, and +28.24 to +44.54 where we are. On the CEO's weights, confirmed, it is +3.37 over hold; on the Board's case, +3.26. It clears the bar and I co-sign it. If it triggers, it is $8B over seven years: about £0.84bn a year, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance, funded from cash, no equity, no leverage. It fits a broadly flat R&D envelope only as redeployment, so nothing widebody runs beside it. Plan for failure: if a selecting airframe later drops us, a 2035 cancel writes off $5.71B, inside the bill.

I withhold my signature on everything else. An unconditional Solo is -0.94 expected and loses the full $8B in S1, S7 and S8. A first Joint Venture commit only costs: -4.00 in S7. UltraFan WB is -3.54 alone, -9.00 beside a trigger. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -0.98 and earns nothing before 2042; beside the conditional it is -5.98, worse than its own bill. Time on wing continues as an other move.

My record is thin on engine-launch economics: these are the board's numbers, not mine. So hold it this way: no cash out unless we are selected, about +3 on paper, nothing booked until a customer is announced. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan NB `launch_if_selected` (2030)
tests.threshold: The engine must be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS, with UltraFan NB ready at launch + 7. If it is launched in or before the airframe's launch round it passes. A zero margin (same round as an NGSA or a 7-year fps) also passes, with a note on the margin; it is neither a fail nor a veto ground. A later launch fails, and that fail is advice only.
tests.numbers: A 2030 trigger makes it ready in 2037 (2030 + 7). Against a 2030 NGSA (EIS 2037) the margin is 0 years. Against a 2030 7-year fps (EIS 2037) it is 0 years. Against a 2030 10-year fps or fps via Embraer (EIS 2040) it is 3 years. No airframe is live on the record, so the test looks forward. The order triggers only if UltraFan would be ready by EIS (rules), so it passes by construction. The zero margin is noted as advice. Test pacing over 7 years with nothing compressed (inference): years 1-2 detailed design, closing gearbox sizing and building on the UltraFan demonstrator; years 3-5 ground and flight test; years 6-7 certification and maturity testing up to EIS. If a phase slips, the engine slips; we do not cut tests. A 2035 UltraFan would be ready in 2042, too late for any 2030 airframe (2037 or 2040), so only this round's conditional can catch a 2030 airframe.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture with P&W
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier only if a folded Solo is further along, as the bulletin shows. It must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves.
tests.numbers: Held this round, and P&W has no commitment on the record. If both sides committed in 2030 (S7) it would form in 2030 and be ready in 2036. Formed in 2035, it is ready in 2041. That is too late for a 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps (2037) and for a 2030 10-year fps (2040). It is in time for a 2035 NGSA or 7-year fps (EIS 2042, 1 year of margin) and a 2035 10-year fps or fps via Embraer (EIS 2045, 4 years). A Solo triggered in 2030 and folded in 2035 would be further along (on its own, ready 2037), so the Joint Venture engine could be ready before 2041. Only the bulletin's date can be used, never one of our own. Under the dashboard rules, Solo spend above RR's $4B share is written off when it folds; McCabe prices that. Folding a Solo would bring years of testing already done, and P&W's gearbox could answer the open gearbox-sizing constraint (inference).

tests.name: Ready by EIS: widebody items (UltraFan WB, Trent 1000 upgrade)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. The Trent 1000 upgrade counts at launch + 3, and not before the first Re-engine's EIS (2042 if neither re-engines).
tests.numbers: Both are held. No Re-engine is on the record. UltraFan WB launched in 2030 would be ready in 2036 but would count only in S8 (Re-engines with EIS 2035), giving -0.90. The upgrade launched in 2030 would count from 2042, or from 2035 in S8, giving -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037 for a 2030 launch), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB, or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture. Nothing on any airframer's dates.
tests.numbers: Draft statement: "Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch." For a 2030 trigger that is 2037, which equals launch + 7, so it passes. It names no airframer date and no ready date for the Joint Venture or UltraFan WB. My advice: do not put 2037 next to NGSA or fps in public, and do not say "ready for [airframe]'s entry into service." The "we don't need partnership for capability" line should not be read as narrowbody support scale. We will need partner shops, and the statement can say so ("support in place with partner shops before entry into service") because the plan below exists.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (briefing constraint). A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (inference).
tests.numbers: Plan for a trigger (inference, built on my record). (1) On trigger in 2030, name partner MRO shops on our Singapore joint-venture model, placed near the selecting airframe's launch operators, without building our own narrowbody MRO scale. (2) Develop repair technology for those shops alongside the test programme, as we did in Singapore. (3) Set up a spares pool and a field-service team for EIS and the early years, so we can respond quickly and intervene. (4) By the 2035 round, contract partner-shop agreements, plus castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers; I report the status in the 2035 test memo. (5) Hold an EIS-readiness review before 2037 (or 2040 for a 10-year fps). It passes only if the CEO carries this plan into the rationale (private, or as a non-public other move). If the plan is missing from the final orders, ground (c) applies at the veto check. It rests on attributed turns.

tests.numbers: Proposed orders (A): no widebody project, so strain is $0 and there are 0 years of overlap. tests.name: Capacity and suppliers

Even a 20% share (a third of Airbus's 60% under code 7, before the +15 pp) is about 800 engines a year (inference). That is about four times our 197 WB engines a year on this board, and well above my midterm OE ramp of 300-350 a year [RX-0279]; 2024 actuals were 529 OE, of which 278 were widebody [R-1295]. Shop visits: I use my 1,100-1,200 total a year [RX-0279], not Helen's 1,400-1,500 [RX-0223], because the figures were never reconciled. Advice: place castings, forgings and gearbox work with high-performing suppliers (GBP 685M of GBP 2.5bn in 2023), not spread it, and build MRO through partner shops. No constraint is reported, so this is not a veto ground.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: 58.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (worst year 58.0%, every year to 2060). A GEnx upgrade (CFM +5 pp) leaves about 53%, still above 50%. S8 (both Re-engines, same EIS) leaves the hold row at +0.00, so Trent stays at 58% (inference from the grid). The case to watch is a lone 787 Re-engine without RR combined with a GEnx upgrade; neither is on the record. Nothing forces widebody spend in 2030. Trent 1000 durability (time on wing) continues as funded.

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would invoke the Civil veto (binding) if the final statement or a public other move gives an EIS or ready date earlier than 2037 for a 2030 UltraFan NB, or names any airframer's dates. I would also invoke it if the rationale drops the partner-shop support plan. I would flag a red-line breach, not a veto, if the upgrade or UltraFan WB is placed beside the conditional. In 2035 I would back widebody spend, upgrade first and within the red lines, if a lone 787 Re-engine appears on the record without RR, or a GEnx upgrade plus a Re-engine put the 50% line at risk. I would test the Joint Venture if P&W's commitment appears on the record (S7): formed in 2035 it is ready in 2041, in time for a 2035 airframe. If the conditional triggers, I would ask the Board to accept that the upgrade waits until the 2045 round. Maturity evidence would also move me: if the UltraFan demonstrator leaves gearbox sizing unresolved, I would press the zero margin against NGSA harder, as advice. A named airframe win on the record would firm up the support build.
ops.memo:
Readiness first. An UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037. Against an NGSA or a 7-year fps launched this year, that's 2037: zero margin. It's a pass with a note, not a veto. Against a 10-year fps or fps via Embraer it's 2040, three years in hand. The conditional only triggers if we're ready by EIS, so the order itself can't compress anything. We're pacing that programme properly: seven years, the full testing schedule, and if a phase slips the engine slips. We don't cut tests.

Support before EIS. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, so the trigger has to carry a partner plan: partner shops on our Singapore joint-venture model, repair technology developed alongside the test programme, and castings and forgings placed with our high-performing suppliers. Tufan, that plan has to be in the rationale. Without it I can't concur on support.

Strain. Nothing widebody this round. The upgrade beside the conditional is -5.98 where it triggers, and UltraFan WB is -9.00. Nobody wants those Trent 1000 blades more than I do, but not while an UltraFan can trigger. Durability work goes on as funded.

Widebody. The brief has us at 58% every year, and a GEnx upgrade takes us to about 53%. Nothing forces spend now.

Statement. "No earlier than seven years from launch" passes. Keep every airframer's date out.

My orders: launch_if_selected, everything else at hold. No Civil veto. We're clearly aligned as one Rolls-Royce, and the fleet keeps flying and earning.

other_moves.move: UltraFan demonstrator path continues
other_moves.detail: UltraFan continues as a technology demonstrator: ground test, public R&D money where available, partner sought. Some of its technology goes into today's Trent fleet for time on wing. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0057, RX-0094, RG-0065].

other_moves.move: Trent 1000 and Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
other_moves.detail: The durability programme (about £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money) continues [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan, ready to activate on trigger (Watson's plan, adopted)
other_moves.detail: If launch_if_selected triggers: (1) name partner MRO shops on our Singapore joint-venture model near the selecting airframe's launch operators, without building our own narrowbody MRO scale [RX-0287]; (2) develop repair technology for those shops alongside the test programme; (3) set up a spares pool and field-service team for EIS and the early years; (4) by the 2035 round, contract the partner-shop agreements and castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers [RX-0286], with Watson reporting status in his 2035 memo; (5) hold an EIS-readiness review before EIS. Test pacing over the full 7 years: years 1-2 detailed design and gearbox sizing, years 3-5 ground and flight test, years 6-7 certification and maturity. If a phase slips, the engine slips; no tests are cut.

other_moves.move: Plan for failure on a triggered programme
other_moves.detail: If the conditional triggers and the selecting airframe later drops our code before EIS, bring a cancel in 2035 (write-off $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B, inside the bill). No orphan programme kept: 'that activity is gone' [R-1573].

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline
other_moves.detail: No price concessions to buy share on any campaign. 'Win-win' terms, value remunerated, every new contract through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.

other_moves.detail: Stated as openness only, in the public statement. No jv_with_pw commitment this round. Revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the public record. Formed then, the Joint Venture is ready in 2041.

decision.public_statement: So, let me be clear. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and only then. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed, and with support in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership is our preference: we are open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, and we are not committing today. Widebody is our franchise. No new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, the decision, by the team rule.

1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL. ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_pw, ultrafan_wb and t1000_upgrade all at hold. Nothing is on the public record: no fps, no NGSA, no Re-engine, no P&W commitment. Only this round's conditional can catch an airframe launched in 2030, because a 2035 UltraFan is ready in 2042, too late for 2037 or 2040.

2. BINDING VETO CHECKS.
- CFO: McCabe co-signs the conditional against the hurdle. The selected columns are +28.24 to +44.54 on an $8B bill, and the expected gain is +3.37 on the weights she confirmed. She withholds her signature on the unconditional Solo, a Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB and the Trent 1000 upgrade (alone or beside the conditional). None of them is ordered. She invokes no balance-sheet veto: no equity, no borrowing, no buyback leverage.
- Civil: Watson invokes no Civil veto. The zero margin of a 2030 trigger (ready 2037) against a 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps (EIS 2037) is a pass with a note. Against a 10-year fps or fps via Embraer (2040) there are three years in hand. The order triggers only if UltraFan is ready by EIS, so nothing is compressed.
- Support: his concurrence rests on the support plan before EIS, carried here and in other_moves. If triggered: partner MRO shops on the Singapore joint-venture model near launch operators, with no own narrowbody MRO scale; repair technology developed alongside the test programme; a spares pool and field-service team for EIS; partner-shop agreements and castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracted with high-performing suppliers by the 2035 round; an EIS-readiness review before EIS. The test pacing is the full seven years: if a phase slips, the engine slips.
- Statement: the public statement gives no EIS earlier than launch + 7, no 2037 next to any airframe, and no airframer date. No veto stands. overrides is empty.

3. GRID, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1/S2/S3/S4/S5/S6/S7/S8). Weights, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.15 (selection 0.10 in total, our rule for 'nothing on the record').
- ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected ('UltraFan NB if selected' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'): 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0. Expected +3.37 (0.05x32.60 + 0.03x28.24 + 0.02x44.54). Board case (0.9 S1, 0.1 S2) +3.26; 0.1 on S4 alone +2.82. Worst column 0. Never below hold under any weights.
- Unconditional Solo instead, against the conditional: -8.00 in S1, S7 and S8, +3.57 in S3 and S6, expected -4.31. Against hold it is -0.94 expected, worst -8.00. Rejected: airframers first [RX-0058], the +$2B bar, McCabe's withheld signature and the Board veto.
- jv_with_pw commit, held ('if selected + commit to JV' minus 'if selected'): 0 everywhere except -4.00 in S7; expected -0.40. P&W has not committed, so a first commit is options management [RX-0051].
- ultrafan_wb launch, held ('if selected + UltraFan WB' minus 'if selected'): -4.00 in S1, S3, S6 and S7; -9.00 in S2, S4 and S5; -0.90 in S8; expected -4.04. No Re-engine is on the record, and the gap is above the $1B sub-cap.
- t1000_upgrade launch, held ('if selected + T1000 upgrade' minus 'if selected'): -0.98 untriggered, -5.98 in S2 and S4, -5.97 in S5, -0.29 in S8; expected -1.38. That is beyond its own $2B bill. Alone ('hold + T1000 upgrade' minus hold) it is -0.88 expected and -0.98 worst, and it would displace the conditional.

4. EXPECTED SCENARIO AND PREMIUM. I expect S1, rivals hold. In S1 the conditional and hold tie at +0.00, the best S1 plan. In expectation the conditional is the best row on the grid, at +3.37. Next come 'if selected + JV' +2.97, 'if selected + upgrade' +1.99, hold 0, 'if selected + UltraFan WB' -0.67 and Solo -0.94. The doctrine-favoured order is also the PV-best order: premium $0B.

5. RED LINES, AGAINST THE FINAL ORDERS. None breached. Both colleagues flagged option D (the upgrade beside launch_if_selected) as a red-line breach. It is struck: not ordered. There is no unconditional launch, no first Joint Venture commit and no UltraFan WB, and no item can lose more than its own bill (worst column 0). There is nothing to cancel.

6. CASH AS AN INPUT [RX-0042].
- Untriggered: £0.
- Triggered: $8B over 7 years, about $1.14B a year, about £0.84bn a year at 1.36 $/£ and about £5.9bn in total. That is 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance of £3.6-3.8bn [R-0222].
- Funding: from free cash flow, as redeployment inside a broadly flat R&D envelope [RX-0214]. It falls after the £7-9bn 2026-28 returns programme. No equity, and no leverage above about 1.5x.
- No widebody development runs beside it. If triggered, the upgrade waits until the 2045 round.

7. TRENT 1000 UPGRADE. My record backs regaining 787 share ('Absolutely' [RX-0101], 'Why not?' [RX-0117]). On this board, though, it earns nothing before 2042 without a Re-engine, and it cannot sit beside the conditional. So it is deferred, not dropped. I revisit it in 2035 if no UltraFan has triggered and a Re-engine is on the record, or as a declared premium within $3B. McCabe would co-sign it then.

8. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. My narrowbody launch record is Medium: words, no launch decision. The conditional form, the +$2B bar and the column weights are company doctrine and inference (profile.md §9; dashboard_game.md §5). The cash figures are McCabe's; readiness, strain and support are Watson's. Frankly, until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing: the conditional commits only when an airframer has chosen us and we can be ready by its EIS.

She gave capex a year if triggered (about £0.84bn, about £5.9bn in total, 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance), funded from FCF as redeployment, with no balance-sheet veto. She withholds her signature on E, F, G, C and D. I order none of them, so her binding vetoes are respected. I adopt her plan for failure (a 2035 cancel, $5.71B write-off, if the selecting airframe drops our code) and her Joint Venture timing (hold to 2035; formed then, ready in 2041). Premium confirmed at $0B. On the upgrade I take her answer: durability stays an other move, and she would co-sign the upgrade later as a declared premium with no UltraFan in play.
memo_weighing.ops: Taken in full. Watson finds the conditional ready by construction: zero margin against a 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps is a pass with a note, and a 10-year fps or fps via Embraer gives three years. I also drop 'we don't need partnership for capability' so it is not read as narrowbody MRO scale. His capacity flag (a narrowbody ramp of about 800 engines a year against 197 widebody) is advice, not a veto. It goes into the 2035 supplier and MRO contracting. Widebody stays at 58%, about 53% under a GEnx upgrade, so nothing forces widebody spend now.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold. No airframer launches a new narrowbody and no Re-engine is announced this round; P&W does not commit. It is the single most likely column, with weight 0.40.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1, 'UltraFan NB: hold' and 'UltraFan NB if selected' tie at +0.00, the best value in the column. 'UltraFan NB if selected' (launch_if_selected, all else hold) is therefore best in S1 and also best in expectation, at +3.37 over hold, because it adds +32.60 / +28.24 / +44.54 in S2, S4 and S5 at no cost elsewhere.
decision.premium_reason: None. The order doctrine favours ('UltraFan NB if selected', everything else at hold) is the best expected grid plan, at +3.37 against +2.97 for the next best ('if selected + JV'). There is no premium for the Trent 1000 upgrade (deferred, up to $0.98B not taken), for UltraFan WB (held; its gap is above the $1B sub-cap) or for narrowbody objective items (the Board allows none).
decision.objective_note:
Briefing goal: enter narrowbody, keep widebody dominance.

Widebody: met. RR stays at 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050, with no widebody order. About 53% under a GEnx upgrade is still above 50%.

Narrowbody: met only if the conditional triggers (S2, S4, S5; weight 0.10). RR then has a narrowbody engine in service from 2037, so its share is above 0 in 2045 and 2050.

The unconditional Solo would also meet it in S3 and S6, through the +15 pp the board credits once any new narrowbody flies, lifting the probability to about 0.35. But that costs -4.31 expected against the conditional, is -8.00 in S1, S7 and S8, breaks the airframers-first red line and draws a Board veto. I pay no premium for the objective: 'We won't do anything not profitable.'

Route left for 2035: if no airframe selects us now, 2035 is the last round whose narrowbody launch can deliver by 2045. That could be a conditional against a 2035 airframe, or the Joint Venture if P&W's commitment is on the record (formed 2035, ready 2041).

- If not triggered: the same conditional discipline in 2035, and test a Joint Venture commit if P&W's commitment is on the record.

recommendations.text: Public statement and other moves: publish the 'open door to Pratt & Whitney' move as openness only. Remove 'Formed then, the Joint Venture is ready in 2041' and any '2035' from its public text. Watson flagged this as a note, not a veto, because 2041 is formation + 6. If the conditional triggers, we want the following at the 2035 review. Watson's report on the partner-shop, castings, forgings and gearbox contracts. The status of gearbox sizing on the demonstrator, since that is the one thing that would turn the zero margin against a 2030 NGSA into a maturity concern. Confirmation that no test phase has been cut to hold 2037: if a phase slips, the engine slips.

If it triggers, McCabe should report the roughly £0.84bn a year (about £5.9bn over seven years) each round against a broadly flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan, with leverage held at or below about 1.5x. Nothing widebody should run beside it: the Trent 1000 upgrade waits for the 2045 round and UltraFan WB stays at hold.
Plan for failure, as adopted: if a selecting airframe drops our code before EIS, bring the 2035 cancel ($8B x 5/7 = $5.71B write-off) rather than keep an orphan programme.

If nothing triggers in 2030, use the same conditional discipline in 2035, the last round whose narrowbody launch can deliver by 2045. Test the Joint Venture only once P&W's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe carries code 2, 4, 6 or 7, and only with a weighted value at or above 0 against the same row without it.

Widebody franchise: the test does not trigger (58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050; no Re-engine on the record). Watch for a rival-engined 787 Re-engine combined with a GEnx upgrade. In a round with no UltraFan in development or ordered, bring the Trent 1000 upgrade within our tests, either against a Re-engine on the record or as a declared premium inside $3B. Keep UltraFan WB at hold until a Re-engine is on the record.
Hold pricing discipline on any campaign: no concessions to buy narrowbody share, win-win terms, value remunerated. Narrowbody is an option, not a need.

Take Watson's capacity advice into the 2035 contracting. A narrowbody ramp of about 800 engines a year is about four times our 197 widebody engines a year on this board. It needs partner MRO and our high-performing suppliers, not capacity spread thin.
